trunks.script: At the 78th Emmy Awards, John Mulaney hosted the event, bringing his signature humor and wit to the stage. Prior to the show, Mariska Hargitay walked the red carpet, exuding grace and elegance. The evening was filled with excitement as winners were interviewed backstage, capturing the essence of the awards ceremony.

source_item.creator: CNBC-TV18
source_item.article_text: Emmys 2026 LIVE: Red Carpet And Backstage Interviews With Emmy Winners | Mariska Hargitay | N18G Emmys 2026 LIVE: Red Carpet And Backstage Interviews With Emmy Winners | Mariska Hargitay | CNBC TV18 LOS ANGELES - All the fashion glitz and glamor from the Emmys red carpet. After the red carpet winners at the Emmy awards speak to the media backstage. Stars of TV and streaming walk the red carpet for the 78th Emmy Awards. Noah Wyle in “The Pitt,” Rhea Seehorn in “Pluribus,” Jean Smart in “Hacks” and Matthew Rhys in “Widow’s Bay” look to be runaway favorites for the top acting awards. The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards take place on September 14, 2026, live from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, hosted by Mariska Hargitay Live interviews with stars as they walk the red carpet ahead of the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards ceremony. Live coverage as stars arrive and walk the red carpet ahead of the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards ceremony. Presenters include Zendaya, Sally Field, Amy Poehler, Jon Hamm, Macaulay Culkin, Alan Cumming, Keke Palmer, Florence Pugh, Marcello Hernández, Odessa A'zion, Dan Levy, Niecy Nash-Betts and “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” stars Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreanaz. Mariska Hargitay will host the event for the first time. Nominees include stars of some of the most talked-about series, such as "The Pitt," "Widow's Bay" and more. The Emmy Awards, being held Monday night at the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles, could propel the medical drama “The Pitt” closer to the Emmy record book. “The Pitt,” HBO Max’s hit hospital show, is the favorite to repeat in the best drama race, and if it wins, it would be the first series to win television’s most prestigious award for its first two seasons since “Mad Men” did it in 2009. The best comedy race, one of the most anticipated categories of the night, will feature a tight showdown between the freshman horror-comedy series “Widow’s Bay” and an Emmy stalwart, “Hacks.” Actors nominated for trophies include Zendaya, Noah Wyle, Sarah Snook and Colman Domingo, while Matthew Rhys, Carey Mulligan and Jack Lowden are among the British nominees. question_answers.question: What is the plot of 'Widow’s Bay' and how does it relate to Matthew Rhys's acting?
question_answers.answer: In 'Widow’s Bay', Matthew Rhys stars as Tom Loftis, the beleaguered mayor of a cursed New England island. The show blends elements of Stephen King and 'The Twilight Zone' with an absurdist sitcom tone and a 'Get Out'-like undertone. Rhys's performance, along with the supporting cast, is praised for its ability to be both funny and frightening in the same scene. Rhys's meme-worthy facial expressions and antics anchor the series, while the surrounding ensemble, including Stephen Root, Kevin Carroll, and Kate O’Flynn, adds depth and strength to the show.

source_item.title: Tesla Model 3 RWD Review 2026 | Best Value Electric Car?
source_item.article_text: Tesla Model 3 RWD Review 2026 | Best Value Electric Car? ![2026 Tesla Model 3 RWD AutoNext In-Depth Review](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fres.cloudinary.com%2Fdzmtsqtky%2Fimage%2Fupload%2Fv1777485224%2FTesla_Model_3_RWD_AutoNext-2_resultaat_oh245g.webp&w=1920&q=75) # 2026 Tesla Model 3 RWD There’s something almost counterintuitive about the Tesla Model 3 Rear-Wheel Drive. The Tesla Model 3 RWD in a few figures: * 283 hp * 420 Nm * 534 km (WLTP) * 13,5 kWh 7,9/10 ##### Notre réseau de concessionnaires Notre vaste réseau de concessionnaires garantit qualité et service. Trouvez un concessionnaire agréé près de chez vous. [Découvrez-les ici](/fr/dealers) Écrit par Rob Van Loock 29/04/2026 ## **The cheapest Tesla might quietly be the smartest EV you can buy.** In a market where electric cars are getting heavier, more complex and significantly more expensive, Tesla strips things back. Less power than the Performance versions, fewer features, a simpler setup and yet, after spending serious time with it, one conclusion keeps coming back: This might be the most rational electric car you can buy right now. Starting at just **€36,990**, it undercuts a large part of the competition. But what makes it interesting isn’t just the price, it’s how little you feel like you’re missing. ### Design: evolution done right With the Highland update, Tesla didn’t try to reinvent the Model 3. Instead, they refined it and that shows. The front end is cleaner and sharper, the lighting slimmer, and the overall design feels more mature than before. It’s still unmistakably a Model 3, but one that has grown up. Less playful, more confident. The RWD version keeps things simple. You get 18-inch aero wheels, a limited selection of exterior colours and no unnecessary visual drama. And honestly, that suits the car perfectly. This was never meant to be a show-off, it’s designed to be efficient, and that philosophy carries through every detail. ### Interior: minimalism, but usable Inside, Tesla continues to do its own thing. Everything is controlled via the central screen. Seats, mirrors, climate settings, it all lives in the interface. At first, that’s not ideal. Adjusting your seat through a touchscreen will never be better than a physical button. But once everything is set, you quickly stop thinking about it. What stands out is how well the system works. It’s fast, logical, and incredibly easy to navigate. Compared to many competitors (especially newer brands trying to impress with endless menus) Tesla keeps things simple. You find what you need almost instantly. There’s no Apple CarPlay, which feels like a miss in the beginning. But Tesla’s own system is so well integrated that after a short time, you stop missing it altogether. ### Build quality: better than expected Tesla hasn’t always had the best reputation when it comes to build quality. Panel gaps, rattles, inconsistent finishes, we’ve all heard the stories. But this Model 3 tells a different story. Everything feels solid. Materials are well assembled, nothing squeaks, nothing feels unfinished. It’s a noticeable step forward, and one that removes a lot of the hesitation people used to have about Tesla. It simply feels like a well-built car now. And that matters. ### Performance: exactly what you need On paper, the numbers are modest compared to the higher-end versions. Around 283 horsepower and 420 Nm of torque. In reality, it’s more than enough. Acceleration is instant, smooth, and perfectly usable in daily driving. It doesn’t try to overwhelm you, but it never feels slow either. The rear-wheel-drive setup adds a layer of balance that makes the car feel natural and predictable. This isn’t about chasing performance figures. It’s about delivering just the right amount of power, exactly when you need it. ### Efficiency: this is where it wins If there’s one area where the Model 3 RWD truly stands out, it’s efficiency. Tesla claims a WLTP range of just over 500 kilometres with a consumption figure around 13 to 14 kWh per 100 kilometres. Normally, you take those numbers with a grain of salt. Here, you don’t have to. Over more than 1,500 kilometres of driving (including a significant amount of highway) we ended up at around **14.5 kWh/100 km**. That’s seriously impressive. Even at higher speeds, the car remains efficient. And that changes everything. Fewer charging stops, lower costs, and most importantly, less stress when driving longer distances. Tesla still sets the benchmark here. ### Comfort and driving: simple, but effective Unlike the more expensive Model 3 versions, this one doesn’t get adaptive or advanced suspension systems. It keeps things simple with a more traditional setup. And yet, it works. The ride is slightly firmer over rougher surfaces, but never uncomfortable. The Tesla Model 3 RWD in a few figures: * 283 hp * 420 Nm * 534 km (WLTP) * 13,5 kWh 7,9/10 ##### Notre réseau de concessionnaires Notre vaste réseau de concessionnaires garantit qualité et service. Trouvez un concessionnaire agréé près de chez vous. [Découvrez-les ici](/fr/dealers) Écrit par Rob Van Loock 29/04/2026 ## **The cheapest Tesla might quietly be the smartest EV you can buy.** In a market where electric cars are getting heavier, more complex and significantly more expensive, Tesla strips things back. Less power than the Performance versions, fewer features, a simpler setup and yet, after spending serious time with it, one conclusion keeps coming back: This might be the most rational electric car you can buy right now. Starting at just **€36,990**, it undercuts a large part of the competition. But what makes it interesting isn’t just the price, it’s how little you feel like you’re missing. ### Design: evolution done right With the Highland update, Tesla didn’t try to reinvent the Model 3. Instead, they refined it and that shows. The front end is cleaner and sharper, the lighting slimmer, and the overall design feels more mature than before. It’s still unmistakably a Model 3, but one that has grown up. Less playful, more confident. The RWD version keeps things simple. You get 18-inch aero wheels, a limited selection of exterior colours and no unnecessary visual drama. And honestly, that suits the car perfectly. This was never meant to be a show-off, it’s designed to be efficient, and that philosophy carries through every detail. ### Interior: minimalism, but usable Inside, Tesla continues to do its own thing. Everything is controlled via the central screen. Seats, mirrors, climate settings, it all lives in the interface. At first, that’s not ideal. Adjusting your seat through a touchscreen will never be better than a physical button. But once everything is set, you quickly stop thinking about it. What stands out is how well the system works. It’s fast, logical, and incredibly easy to navigate. Compared to many competitors (especially newer brands trying to impress with endless menus) Tesla keeps things simple. You find what you need almost instantly. There’s no Apple CarPlay, which feels like a miss in the beginning. But Tesla’s own system is so well integrated that after a short time, you stop missing it altogether. ### Build quality: better than expected Tesla hasn’t always had the best reputation when it comes to build quality. Panel gaps, rattles, inconsistent finishes, we’ve all heard the stories. But this Model 3 tells a different story. Everything feels solid. Materials are well assembled, nothing squeaks, nothing feels unfinished. It’s a noticeable step forward, and one that removes a lot of the hesitation people used to have about Tesla. It simply feels like a well-built car now. And that matters. ### Performance: exactly what you need On paper, the numbers are modest compared to the higher-end versions. Around 283 horsepower and 420 Nm of torque. In reality, it’s more than enough. Acceleration is instant, smooth, and perfectly usable in daily driving. It doesn’t try to overwhelm you, but it never feels slow either. The rear-wheel-drive setup adds a layer of balance that makes the car feel natural and predictable. This isn’t about chasing performance figures. It’s about delivering just the right amount of power, exactly when you need it. ### Efficiency: this is where it wins If there’s one area where the Model 3 RWD truly stands out, it’s efficiency. Tesla claims a WLTP range of just over 500 kilometres with a consumption figure around 13 to 14 kWh per 100 kilometres. Normally, you take those numbers with a grain of salt. Here, you don’t have to. Over more than 1,500 kilometres of driving (including a significant amount of highway) we ended up at around **14.5 kWh/100 km**. That’s seriously impressive. Even at higher speeds, the car remains efficient. And that changes everything. Fewer charging stops, lower costs, and most importantly, less stress when driving longer distances. Tesla still sets the benchmark here. ### Comfort and driving: simple, but effective Unlike the more expensive Model 3 versions, this one doesn’t get adaptive or advanced suspension systems. It keeps things simple with a more traditional setup. And yet, it works. The ride is slightly firmer over rougher surfaces, but never uncomfortable. The 18-inch wheels help absorb imperfections, and overall the car feels composed and stable. It’s not trying to be sporty, but it’s not boring either. The rear-wheel drive gives it just enough character to make it enjoyable on a twisty road, without ever becoming demanding. Exactly what most people actually want. ### Everyday usability: still one of the best As a daily car, the Model 3 continues to make a strong case for itself. The seating position works well, even for taller drivers. Rear passengers have enough space, and the combination of rear trunk and front storage makes it more practical than you might expect from a sedan. It’s not trying to be an SUV and that’s part of its strength. It stays efficient, low, and well balanced. Tesla’s biggest advantage isn’t just the tech itself, it’s how easy it is to use. Everything feels immediate and logical. Navigation is fast, settings are easy to access, and even small things (like disabling warning sounds) can be done in seconds. Where other brands often overcomplicate things, Tesla simplifies them. And that makes a huge difference in daily use. ### Price: the real game changer At €36,990, the Model 3 RWD sits in a space where competition becomes difficult. Because when you combine: efficiency, range, technology and overall usability, there’s simply not much that matches it at this price point. And that’s what makes it so strong. ### AutoNext Verdict The Tesla Model 3 RWD (2026) isn’t the most exciting electric car. It’s not the fastest, not the most luxurious, and not the most emotional. But it might be the smartest. It focuses on what actually matters and executes it exceptionally well. The efficiency is outstanding, the range is realistic, the build quality has improved, and the technology remains one of the easiest to live with. Yes, there are compromises. The lack of physical controls, the absence of CarPlay, the more basic equipment level, you notice them. But they fade quickly once you start living with the car. Because the bigger picture is simply too strong. **For this price, this might be the best all-round electric car you can buy today.** ![Mercedes-Benz EQB 250](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fa.storyblok.com%2Ff%2F286419086467324%2F6912x4608%2F47cbc1c3f1%2Fset1cjw03263.webp&w=1920&q=75)7,7/10 Avis 01/12/2025 ### Mercedes-Benz EQB 250 Twenty or so years ago, the battery electric vehicle (BEV) arms race began with exotic vehicles of all sorts, cars like the Tesla Roadster or the more recent Jaguar I-Pace. But thankfully, the world is now being fed regular models powered by batteries too, and today's subject is one of those: the Mercedes EQB 250 Luxury Line. When the Skoda Enyaq launched, it proved that this philosophy could also work in the electric era. Now Skoda takes the next step with the **all-new Skoda Elroq**, a compact electric SUV positioned below the Enyaq in the lineup. Smaller, more city-friendly and slightly more affordable, but still built on the same advanced Volkswagen Group MEB platform. [Lire l'article complet](/fr/reviews/skoda/2025-skoda-elroq-85-corporate) ![2026 BYD Seal](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fres.cloudinary.com%2Fdzmtsqtky%2Fimage%2Fupload%2Fv1774123415%2FFAT-ICE-Retromobile-2026-185_resultaat_ditjrl.webp&w=1920&q=75)6,7/10 Avis 21/03/2026 ### 2026 BYD Seal Some cars only reveal their true character when you put them through far too many kilometres in far too little time. The **BYD Seal Excellence AWD** is exactly that kind of car. No neat half-day test drive, no predictable loop around the block (but over 3,200 kilometres in a single week, including more than 2,200 kilometres in just 48 hours. Austria, Paris, back home) highways, cold nights, charging stops, detours, stress, fatigue, and above all: plenty of time to discover where a car truly excels… and where it doesn’t. [Découvrez-les ici](/fr/dealers) Écrit par Rob Van Loock 29/04/2026 ## **The cheapest Tesla might quietly be the smartest EV you can buy.** In a market where electric cars are getting heavier, more complex and significantly more expensive, Tesla strips things back. Less power than the Performance versions, fewer features, a simpler setup and yet, after spending serious time with it, one conclusion keeps coming back: This might be the most rational electric car you can buy right now. Starting at just **€36,990**, it undercuts a large part of the competition. But what makes it interesting isn’t just the price, it’s how little you feel like you’re missing. ### Design: evolution done right With the Highland update, Tesla didn’t try to reinvent the Model 3. Instead, they refined it and that shows. The front end is cleaner and sharper, the lighting slimmer, and the overall design feels more mature than before. It’s still unmistakably a Model 3, but one that has grown up. Less playful, more confident. The RWD version keeps things simple. You get 18-inch aero wheels, a limited selection of exterior colours and no unnecessary visual drama. And honestly, that suits the car perfectly. This was never meant to be a show-off, it’s designed to be efficient, and that philosophy carries through every detail. ### Interior: minimalism, but usable Inside, Tesla continues to do its own thing. Everything is controlled via the central screen. Seats, mirrors, climate settings, it all lives in the interface. At first, that’s not ideal. Adjusting your seat through a touchscreen will never be better than a physical button. But once everything is set, you quickly stop thinking about it. What stands out is how well the system works. It’s fast, logical, and incredibly easy to navigate. Compared to many competitors (especially newer brands trying to impress with endless menus) Tesla keeps things simple. You find what you need almost instantly. There’s no Apple CarPlay, which feels like a miss in the beginning. But Tesla’s own system is so well integrated that after a short time, you stop missing it altogether. ### Build quality: better than expected Tesla hasn’t always had the best reputation when it comes to build quality. Panel gaps, rattles, inconsistent finishes, we’ve all heard the stories. But this Model 3 tells a different story. Everything feels solid. Materials are well assembled, nothing squeaks, nothing feels unfinished. It’s a noticeable step forward, and one that removes a lot of the hesitation people used to have about Tesla. It simply feels like a well-built car now. And that matters. ### Performance: exactly what you need On paper, the numbers are modest compared to the higher-end versions. Around 283 horsepower and 420 Nm of torque. In reality, it’s more than enough. Acceleration is instant, smooth, and perfectly usable in daily driving. It doesn’t try to overwhelm you, but it never feels slow either. The rear-wheel-drive setup adds a layer of balance that makes the car feel natural and predictable. This isn’t about chasing performance figures. It’s about delivering just the right amount of power, exactly when you need it. ### Efficiency: this is where it wins If there’s one area where the Model 3 RWD truly stands out, it’s efficiency. Tesla claims a WLTP range of just over 500 kilometres with a consumption figure around 13 to 14 kWh per 100 kilometres. Normally, you take those numbers with a grain of salt. Here, you don’t have to. Over more than 1,500 kilometres of driving (including a significant amount of highway) we ended up at around **14.5 kWh/100 km**. That’s seriously impressive. Even at higher speeds, the car remains efficient. And that changes everything. Fewer charging stops, lower costs, and most importantly, less stress when driving longer distances. Tesla still sets the benchmark here. ### Comfort and driving: simple, but effective Unlike the more expensive Model 3 versions, this one doesn’t get adaptive or advanced suspension systems. It keeps things simple with a more traditional setup. And yet, it works. The ride is slightly firmer over rougher surfaces, but never uncomfortable. The 18-inch wheels help absorb imperfections, and overall the car feels composed and stable. It’s not trying to be sporty, but it’s not boring either. The rear-wheel drive gives it just enough character to make it enjoyable on a twisty road, without ever becoming demanding. Exactly what most people actually want. ### Everyday usability: still one of the best As a daily car, the Model 3 continues to make a strong case for itself. The seating position works well, even for taller drivers. Rear passengers have enough space, and the combination of rear trunk and front storage makes it more practical than you might expect from a sedan. It’s not trying to be an SUV and that’s part of its strength. It stays efficient, low, and well balanced. Tesla’s biggest advantage isn’t just the tech itself, it’s how easy it is to use. Everything feels immediate and logical. Navigation is fast, settings are easy to access, and even small things (like disabling warning sounds) can be done in seconds. Where other brands often overcomplicate things, Tesla simplifies them. And that makes a huge difference in daily use. ### Price: the real game changer At €36,990, the Model 3 RWD sits in a space where competition becomes difficult. Because when you combine: efficiency, range, technology and overall usability, there’s simply not much that matches it at this price point. And that’s what makes it so strong. ### AutoNext Verdict The Tesla Model 3 RWD (2026) isn’t the most exciting electric car. It’s not the fastest, not the most luxurious, and not the most emotional. But it might be the smartest. It focuses on what actually matters and executes it exceptionally well. The efficiency is outstanding, the range is realistic, the build quality has improved, and the technology remains one of the easiest to live with. Yes, there are compromises. The lack of physical controls, the absence of CarPlay, the more basic equipment level, you notice them. But they fade quickly once you start living with the car. Because the bigger picture is simply too strong. **For this price, this might be the best all-round electric car you can buy today.** ![Mercedes-Benz EQB 250](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fa.storyblok.com%2Ff%2F286419086467324%2F6912x4608%2F47cbc1c3f1%2Fset1cjw03263.webp&w=1920&q=75)7,7/10 Avis 01/12/2025 ### Mercedes-Benz EQB 250 Twenty or so years ago, the battery electric vehicle (BEV) arms race began with exotic vehicles of all sorts, cars like the Tesla Roadster or the more recent Jaguar I-Pace. But thankfully, the world is now being fed regular models powered by batteries too, and today's subject is one of those: the Mercedes EQB 250 Luxury Line. [Découvrez-les ici](/fr/dealers) Écrit par Rob Van Loock 29/04/2026 ## **The cheapest Tesla might quietly be the smartest EV you can buy.** In a market where electric cars are getting heavier, more complex and significantly more expensive, Tesla strips things back. Less power than the Performance versions, fewer features, a simpler setup and yet, after spending serious time with it, one conclusion keeps coming back: This might be the most rational electric car you can buy right now. Starting at just **€36,990**, it undercuts a large part of the competition. But what makes it interesting isn’t just the price, it’s how little you feel like you’re missing. ### Design: evolution done right With the Highland update, Tesla didn’t try to reinvent the Model 3. Instead, they refined it and that shows. The front end is cleaner and sharper, the lighting slimmer, and the overall design feels more mature than before. It’s still unmistakably a Model 3, but one that has grown up. Less playful, more confident. The RWD version keeps things simple. You get 18-inch aero wheels, a limited selection of exterior colours and no unnecessary visual drama. And honestly, that suits the car perfectly. This was never meant to be a show-off, it’s designed to be efficient, and that philosophy carries through every detail. ### Interior: minimalism, but usable Inside, Tesla continues to do its own thing. Everything is controlled via the central screen. Seats, mirrors, climate settings, it all lives in the interface. At first, that’s not ideal. Adjusting your seat through a touchscreen will never be better than a physical button. But once everything is set, you quickly stop thinking about it. What stands out is how well the system works. It’s fast, logical, and incredibly easy to navigate. Compared to many competitors (especially newer brands trying to impress with endless menus) Tesla keeps things simple. You find what you need almost instantly. There’s no Apple CarPlay, which feels like a miss in the beginning. But Tesla’s own system is so well integrated that after a short time, you stop missing it altogether. ### Build quality: better than expected Tesla hasn’t always had the best reputation when it comes to build quality. Panel gaps, rattles, inconsistent finishes, we’ve all heard the stories. But this Model 3 tells a different story. Everything feels solid. Materials are well assembled, nothing squeaks, nothing feels unfinished. It’s a noticeable step forward, and one that removes a lot of the hesitation people used to have about Tesla. It simply feels like a well-built car now. And that matters. ### Performance: exactly what you need On paper, the numbers are modest compared to the higher-end versions. Around 283 horsepower and 420 Nm of torque. In reality, it’s more than enough. Acceleration is instant, smooth, and perfectly usable in daily driving. It doesn’t try to overwhelm you, but it never feels slow either. The rear-wheel-drive setup adds a layer of balance that makes the car feel natural and predictable. This isn’t about chasing performance figures. It’s about delivering just the right amount of power, exactly when you need it. ### Efficiency: this is where it wins If there’s one area where the Model 3 RWD truly stands out, it’s efficiency. Tesla claims a WLTP range of just over 500 kilometres with a consumption figure around 13 to 14 kWh per 100 kilometres. Normally, you take those numbers with a grain of salt. Here, you don’t have to. Over more than 1,500 kilometres of driving (including a significant amount of highway) we ended up at around **14.5 kWh/100 km**. That’s seriously impressive. Even at higher speeds, the car remains efficient. And that changes everything. Fewer charging stops, lower costs, and most importantly, less stress when driving longer distances. Tesla still sets the benchmark here. ### Comfort and driving: simple, but effective Unlike the more expensive Model 3 versions, this one doesn’t get adaptive or advanced suspension systems. It keeps things simple with a more traditional setup. And yet, it works. The ride is slightly firmer over rougher surfaces, but never uncomfortable. The 18-inch wheels help absorb imperfections, and overall the car feels composed and stable. It’s not trying to be sporty, but it’s not boring either. The rear-wheel drive gives it just enough character to make it enjoyable on a twisty road, without ever becoming demanding. Exactly what most people actually want. ### Everyday usability: still one of the best As a daily car, the Model 3 continues to make a strong case for itself. The seating position works well, even for taller drivers. Rear passengers have enough space, and the combination of rear trunk and front storage makes it more practical than you might expect from a sedan. It’s not trying to be an SUV and that’s part of its strength. It stays efficient, low, and well balanced. Tesla’s biggest advantage isn’t just the tech itself, it’s how easy it is to use. Everything feels immediate and logical. Navigation is fast, settings are easy to access, and even small things (like disabling warning sounds) can be done in seconds. Where other brands often overcomplicate things, Tesla simplifies them. And that makes a huge difference in daily use. ### Price: the real game changer At €36,990, the Model 3 RWD sits in a space where competition becomes difficult. Because when you combine: efficiency, range, technology and overall usability, there’s simply not much that matches it at this price point. And that’s what makes it so strong. ### AutoNext Verdict The Tesla Model 3 RWD (2026) isn’t the most exciting electric car. It’s not the fastest, not the most luxurious, and not the most emotional. But it might be the smartest. It focuses on what actually matters and executes it exceptionally well. The efficiency is outstanding, the range is realistic, the build quality has improved, and the technology remains one of the easiest to live with. Yes, there are compromises. The lack of physical controls, the absence of CarPlay, the more basic equipment level, you notice them. But they fade quickly once you start living with the car. Because the bigger picture is simply too strong. **For this price, this might be the best all-round electric car you can buy today.** ![Mercedes-Benz EQB 250](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fa.storyblok.com%2Ff%2F286419086467324%2F6912x4608%2F47cbc1c3f1%2Fset1cjw03263.webp&w=1920&q=75)7,7/10 Avis 01/12/2025 ### Mercedes-Benz EQB 250 Twenty or so years ago, the battery electric vehicle (BEV) arms race began with exotic vehicles of all sorts, cars like the Tesla Roadster or the more recent Jaguar I-Pace. But thankfully, the world is now being fed regular models powered by batteries too, and today's subject is one of those: the Mercedes EQB 250 Luxury Line. When the Skoda Enyaq launched, it proved that this philosophy could also work in the electric era. Now Skoda takes the next step with the **all-new Skoda Elroq**, a compact electric SUV positioned below the Enyaq in the lineup. Smaller, more city-friendly and slightly more affordable, but still built on the same advanced Volkswagen Group MEB platform. The **BYD Seal Excellence AWD** is exactly that kind of car. No neat half-day test drive, no predictable loop around the block (but over 3,200 kilometres in a single week, including more than 2,200 kilometres in just 48 hours. Austria, Paris, back home) highways, cold nights, charging stops, detours, stress, fatigue, and above all: plenty of time to discover where a car truly excels… and where it doesn’t. source_item.article_text: Tesla Model 3 RWD Review 2026 | Best Value Electric Car? ![2026 Tesla Model 3 RWD AutoNext In-Depth Review](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fres.cloudinary.com%2Fdzmtsqtky%2Fimage%2Fupload%2Fv1777485224%2FTesla_Model_3_RWD_AutoNext-2_resultaat_oh245g.webp&w=1920&q=75) # 2026 Tesla Model 3 RWD There’s something almost counterintuitive about the Tesla Model 3 Rear-Wheel Drive. The Tesla Model 3 RWD in a few figures: * 283 hp * 420 Nm * 534 km (WLTP) * 13,5 kWh 7,9/10 ##### Notre réseau de concessionnaires Notre vaste réseau de concessionnaires garantit qualité et service. Trouvez un concessionnaire agréé près de chez vous. [Découvrez-les ici](/fr/dealers) Écrit par Rob Van Loock 29/04/2026 ## **The cheapest Tesla might quietly be the smartest EV you can buy.** In a market where electric cars are getting heavier, more complex and significantly more expensive, Tesla strips things back. Less power than the Performance versions, fewer features, a simpler setup and yet, after spending serious time with it, one conclusion keeps coming back: This might be the most rational electric car you can buy right now. Starting at just **€36,990**, it undercuts a large part of the competition. But what makes it interesting isn’t just the price, it’s how little you feel like you’re missing. ### Design: evolution done right With the Highland update, Tesla didn’t try to reinvent the Model 3. Instead, they refined it and that shows. The front end is cleaner and sharper, the lighting slimmer, and the overall design feels more mature than before. It’s still unmistakably a Model 3, but one that has grown up. Less playful, more confident. The RWD version keeps things simple. You get 18-inch aero wheels, a limited selection of exterior colours and no unnecessary visual drama. And honestly, that suits the car perfectly. This was never meant to be a show-off, it’s designed to be efficient, and that philosophy carries through every detail. ### Interior: minimalism, but usable Inside, Tesla continues to do its own thing. Everything is controlled via the central screen. Seats, mirrors, climate settings, it all lives in the interface. At first, that’s not ideal. Adjusting your seat through a touchscreen will never be better than a physical button. But once everything is set, you quickly stop thinking about it. What stands out is how well the system works. It’s fast, logical, and incredibly easy to navigate. Compared to many competitors (especially newer brands trying to impress with endless menus) Tesla keeps things simple. You find what you need almost instantly. There’s no Apple CarPlay, which feels like a miss in the beginning. But Tesla’s own system is so well integrated that after a short time, you stop missing it altogether. ### Build quality: better than expected Tesla hasn’t always had the best reputation when it comes to build quality. Panel gaps, rattles, inconsistent finishes, we’ve all heard the stories. But this Model 3 tells a different story. Everything feels solid. Materials are well assembled, nothing squeaks, nothing feels unfinished. It’s a noticeable step forward, and one that removes a lot of the hesitation people used to have about Tesla. It simply feels like a well-built car now. And that matters. ### Performance: exactly what you need On paper, the numbers are modest compared to the higher-end versions. Around 283 horsepower and 420 Nm of torque. In reality, it’s more than enough. Acceleration is instant, smooth, and perfectly usable in daily driving. It doesn’t try to overwhelm you, but it never feels slow either. The rear-wheel-drive setup adds a layer of balance that makes the car feel natural and predictable. This isn’t about chasing performance figures. It’s about delivering just the right amount of power, exactly when you need it. ### Efficiency: this is where it wins If there’s one area where the Model 3 RWD truly stands out, it’s efficiency. Tesla claims a WLTP range of just over 500 kilometres with a consumption figure around 13 to 14 kWh per 100 kilometres. Normally, you take those numbers with a grain of salt. Here, you don’t have to. Over more than 1,500 kilometres of driving (including a significant amount of highway) we ended up at around **14.5 kWh/100 km**. That’s seriously impressive. Even at higher speeds, the car remains efficient. And that changes everything. Fewer charging stops, lower costs, and most importantly, less stress when driving longer distances. Tesla still sets the benchmark here. ### Comfort and driving: simple, but effective Unlike the more expensive Model 3 versions, this one doesn’t get adaptive or advanced suspension systems. It keeps things simple with a more traditional setup. And yet, it works. The ride is slightly firmer over rougher surfaces, but never uncomfortable. The 18-inch wheels help absorb imperfections, and overall the car feels composed and stable. It’s not trying to be sporty, but it’s not boring either. The rear-wheel drive gives it just enough character to make it enjoyable on a twisty road, without ever becoming demanding. Exactly what most people actually want. ### Everyday usability: still one of the best As a daily car, the Model 3 continues to make a strong case for itself. The seating position works well, even for taller drivers. Rear passengers have enough space, and the combination of rear trunk and front storage makes it more practical than you might expect from a sedan. It’s not trying to be an SUV and that’s part of its strength. It stays efficient, low, and well balanced. Tesla’s biggest advantage isn’t just the tech itself, it’s how easy it is to use. Everything feels immediate and logical. Navigation is fast, settings are easy to access, and even small things (like disabling warning sounds) can be done in seconds. Where other brands often overcomplicate things, Tesla simplifies them. And that makes a huge difference in daily use. ### Price: the real game changer At €36,990, the Model 3 RWD sits in a space where competition becomes difficult. Because when you combine: efficiency, range, technology and overall usability, there’s simply not much that matches it at this price point. And that’s what makes it so strong. ### AutoNext Verdict The Tesla Model 3 RWD (2026) isn’t the most exciting electric car. It’s not the fastest, not the most luxurious, and not the most emotional. But it might be the smartest. It focuses on what actually matters and executes it exceptionally well. The efficiency is outstanding, the range is realistic, the build quality has improved, and the technology remains one of the easiest to live with. Yes, there are compromises. The lack of physical controls, the absence of CarPlay, the more basic equipment level, you notice them. But they fade quickly once you start living with the car. Because the bigger picture is simply too strong. **For this price, this might be the best all-round electric car you can buy today.** ![Mercedes-Benz EQB 250](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fa.storyblok.com%2Ff%2F286419086467324%2F6912x4608%2F47cbc1c3f1%2Fset1cjw03263.webp&w=1920&q=75)7,7/10 Avis 01/12/2025 ### Mercedes-Benz EQB 250 Twenty or so years ago, the battery electric vehicle (BEV) arms race began with exotic vehicles of all sorts, cars like the Tesla Roadster or the more recent Jaguar I-Pace. But thankfully, the world is now being fed regular models powered by batteries too, and today's subject is one of those: the Mercedes EQB 250 Luxury Line. When the Skoda Enyaq launched, it proved that this philosophy could also work in the electric era. Now Skoda takes the next step with the **all-new Skoda Elroq**, a compact electric SUV positioned below the Enyaq in the lineup. Smaller, more city-friendly and slightly more affordable, but still built on the same advanced Volkswagen Group MEB platform. [Lire l'article complet](/fr/reviews/skoda/2025-skoda-elroq-85-corporate) ![2026 BYD Seal](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fres.cloudinary.com%2Fdzmtsqtky%2Fimage%2Fupload%2Fv1774123415%2FFAT-ICE-Retromobile-2026-185_resultaat_ditjrl.webp&w=1920&q=75)6,7/10 Avis 21/03/2026 ### 2026 BYD Seal Some cars only reveal their true character when you put them through far too many kilometres in far too little time. The **BYD Seal Excellence AWD** is exactly that kind of car. No neat half-day test drive, no predictable loop around the block (but over 3,200 kilometres in a single week, including more than 2,200 kilometres in just 48 hours. Austria, Paris, back home) highways, cold nights, charging stops, detours, stress, fatigue, and above all: plenty of time to discover where a car truly excels… and where it doesn’t. The Tesla Model 3 RWD in a few figures: * 283 hp * 420 Nm * 534 km (WLTP) * 13,5 kWh 7,9/10 ##### Notre réseau de concessionnaires Notre vaste réseau de concessionnaires garantit qualité et service. Trouvez un concessionnaire agréé près de chez vous. [Découvrez-les ici](/fr/dealers) Écrit par Rob Van Loock 29/04/2026 ## **The cheapest Tesla might quietly be the smartest EV you can buy.** In a market where electric cars are getting heavier, more complex and significantly more expensive, Tesla strips things back. Less power than the Performance versions, fewer features, a simpler setup and yet, after spending serious time with it, one conclusion keeps coming back: This might be the most rational electric car you can buy right now. Starting at just **€36,990**, it undercuts a large part of the competition. But what makes it interesting isn’t just the price, it’s how little you feel like you’re missing. ### Design: evolution done right With the Highland update, Tesla didn’t try to reinvent the Model 3. Instead, they refined it and that shows. The front end is cleaner and sharper, the lighting slimmer, and the overall design feels more mature than before. It’s still unmistakably a Model 3, but one that has grown up. Less playful, more confident. The RWD version keeps things simple. You get 18-inch aero wheels, a limited selection of exterior colours and no unnecessary visual drama. And honestly, that suits the car perfectly. This was never meant to be a show-off, it’s designed to be efficient, and that philosophy carries through every detail. ### Interior: minimalism, but usable Inside, Tesla continues to do its own thing. Everything is controlled via the central screen. Seats, mirrors, climate settings, it all lives in the interface. At first, that’s not ideal. Adjusting your seat through a touchscreen will never be better than a physical button. But once everything is set, you quickly stop thinking about it. What stands out is how well the system works. It’s fast, logical, and incredibly easy to navigate. Compared to many competitors (especially newer brands trying to impress with endless menus) Tesla keeps things simple. You find what you need almost instantly. There’s no Apple CarPlay, which feels like a miss in the beginning. But Tesla’s own system is so well integrated that after a short time, you stop missing it altogether. ### Build quality: better than expected Tesla hasn’t always had the best reputation when it comes to build quality. Panel gaps, rattles, inconsistent finishes, we’ve all heard the stories. But this Model 3 tells a different story. Everything feels solid. Materials are well assembled, nothing squeaks, nothing feels unfinished. It’s a noticeable step forward, and one that removes a lot of the hesitation people used to have about Tesla. It simply feels like a well-built car now. And that matters. ### Performance: exactly what you need On paper, the numbers are modest compared to the higher-end versions. Around 283 horsepower and 420 Nm of torque. In reality, it’s more than enough. Acceleration is instant, smooth, and perfectly usable in daily driving. It doesn’t try to overwhelm you, but it never feels slow either. The rear-wheel-drive setup adds a layer of balance that makes the car feel natural and predictable. This isn’t about chasing performance figures. It’s about delivering just the right amount of power, exactly when you need it. ### Efficiency: this is where it wins If there’s one area where the Model 3 RWD truly stands out, it’s efficiency. Tesla claims a WLTP range of just over 500 kilometres with a consumption figure around 13 to 14 kWh per 100 kilometres. Normally, you take those numbers with a grain of salt. Here, you don’t have to. Over more than 1,500 kilometres of driving (including a significant amount of highway) we ended up at around **14.5 kWh/100 km**. That’s seriously impressive. Even at higher speeds, the car remains efficient. And that changes everything. Fewer charging stops, lower costs, and most importantly, less stress when driving longer distances. Tesla still sets the benchmark here. ### Comfort and driving: simple, but effective Unlike the more expensive Model 3 versions, this one doesn’t get adaptive or advanced suspension systems. It keeps things simple with a more traditional setup. And yet, it works. The ride is slightly firmer over rougher surfaces, but never uncomfortable. The 18-inch wheels help absorb imperfections, and overall the car feels composed and stable. It’s not trying to be sporty, but it’s not boring either. The rear-wheel drive gives it just enough character to make it enjoyable on a twisty road, without ever becoming demanding. Exactly what most people actually want. ### Everyday usability: still one of the best As a daily car, the Model 3 continues to make a strong case for itself. The seating position works well, even for taller drivers. Rear passengers have enough space, and the combination of rear trunk and front storage makes it more practical than you might expect from a sedan. It’s not trying to be an SUV and that’s part of its strength. It stays efficient, low, and well balanced. Tesla’s biggest advantage isn’t just the tech itself, it’s how easy it is to use. Everything feels immediate and logical. Navigation is fast, settings are easy to access, and even small things (like disabling warning sounds) can be done in seconds. Where other brands often overcomplicate things, Tesla simplifies them. And that makes a huge difference in daily use. ### Price: the real game changer At €36,990, the Model 3 RWD sits in a space where competition becomes difficult. Because when you combine: efficiency, range, technology and overall usability, there’s simply not much that matches it at this price point. And that’s what makes it so strong. ### AutoNext Verdict The Tesla Model 3 RWD (2026) isn’t the most exciting electric car. It’s not the fastest, not the most luxurious, and not the most emotional. But it might be the smartest. It focuses on what actually matters and executes it exceptionally well. The efficiency is outstanding, the range is realistic, the build quality has improved, and the technology remains one of the easiest to live with. Yes, there are compromises. The lack of physical controls, the absence of CarPlay, the more basic equipment level, you notice them. But they fade quickly once you start living with the car. Because the bigger picture is simply too strong. **For this price, this might be the best all-round electric car you can buy today.** ![Mercedes-Benz EQB 250](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fa.storyblok.com%2Ff%2F286419086467324%2F6912x4608%2F47cbc1c3f1%2Fset1cjw03263.webp&w=1920&q=75)7,7/10 Avis 01/12/2025 ### Mercedes-Benz EQB 250 Twenty or so years ago, the battery electric vehicle (BEV) arms race began with exotic vehicles of all sorts, cars like the Tesla Roadster or the more recent Jaguar I-Pace. But thankfully, the world is now being fed regular models powered by batteries too, and today's subject is one of those: the Mercedes EQB 250 Luxury Line. When the Skoda Enyaq launched, it proved that this philosophy could also work in the electric era. Now Skoda takes the next step with the **all-new Skoda Elroq**, a compact electric SUV positioned below the Enyaq in the lineup. Smaller, more city-friendly and slightly more affordable, but still built on the same advanced Volkswagen Group MEB platform. [Lire l'article complet](/fr/reviews/skoda/2025-skoda-elroq-85-corporate) ![2026 BYD Seal](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fres.cloudinary.com%2Fdzmtsqtky%2Fimage%2Fupload%2Fv1774123415%2FFAT-ICE-Retromobile-2026-185_resultaat_ditjrl.webp&w=1920&q=75)6,7/10 Avis 21/03/2026 ### 2026 BYD Seal Some cars only reveal their true character when you put them through far too many kilometres in far too little time. The **BYD Seal Excellence AWD** is exactly that kind of car. No neat half-day test drive, no predictable loop around the block (but over 3,200 kilometres in a single week, including more than 2,200 kilometres in just 48 hours. Austria, Paris, back home) highways, cold nights, charging stops, detours, stress, fatigue, and above all: plenty of time to discover where a car truly excels… and where it doesn’t. [Découvrez-les ici](/fr/dealers) Écrit par Rob Van Loock 29/04/2026 ## **The cheapest Tesla might quietly be the smartest EV you can buy.** In a market where electric cars are getting heavier, more complex and significantly more expensive, Tesla strips things back. Less power than the Performance versions, fewer features, a simpler setup and yet, after spending serious time with it, one conclusion keeps coming back: This might be the most rational electric car you can buy right now. Starting at just **€36,990**, it undercuts a large part of the competition. But what makes it interesting isn’t just the price, it’s how little you feel like you’re missing. ### Design: evolution done right With the Highland update, Tesla didn’t try to reinvent the Model 3. Instead, they refined it and that shows. The front end is cleaner and sharper, the lighting slimmer, and the overall design feels more mature than before. It’s still unmistakably a Model 3, but one that has grown up. Less playful, more confident. The RWD version keeps things simple. You get 18-inch aero wheels, a limited selection of exterior colours and no unnecessary visual drama. And honestly, that suits the car perfectly. This was never meant to be a show-off, it’s designed to be efficient, and that philosophy carries through every detail. ### Interior: minimalism, but usable Inside, Tesla continues to do its own thing. Everything is controlled via the central screen. Seats, mirrors, climate settings, it all lives in the interface. At first, that’s not ideal. Adjusting your seat through a touchscreen will never be better than a physical button. But once everything is set, you quickly stop thinking about it. What stands out is how well the system works. It’s fast, logical, and incredibly easy to navigate. Compared to many competitors (especially newer brands trying to impress with endless menus) Tesla keeps things simple. You find what you need almost instantly. There’s no Apple CarPlay, which feels like a miss in the beginning. But Tesla’s own system is so well integrated that after a short time, you stop missing it altogether. ### Build quality: better than expected Tesla hasn’t always had the best reputation when it comes to build quality. Panel gaps, rattles, inconsistent finishes, we’ve all heard the stories. But this Model 3 tells a different story. Everything feels solid. Materials are well assembled, nothing squeaks, nothing feels unfinished. It’s a noticeable step forward, and one that removes a lot of the hesitation people used to have about Tesla. It simply feels like a well-built car now. And that matters. ### Performance: exactly what you need On paper, the numbers are modest compared to the higher-end versions. Around 283 horsepower and 420 Nm of torque. In reality, it’s more than enough. Acceleration is instant, smooth, and perfectly usable in daily driving. It doesn’t try to overwhelm you, but it never feels slow either. The rear-wheel-drive setup adds a layer of balance that makes the car feel natural and predictable. This isn’t about chasing performance figures. It’s about delivering just the right amount of power, exactly when you need it. ### Efficiency: this is where it wins If there’s one area where the Model 3 RWD truly stands out, it’s efficiency. Tesla claims a WLTP range of just over 500 kilometres with a consumption figure around 13 to 14 kWh per 100 kilometres. Normally, you take those numbers with a grain of salt. Here, you don’t have to. Over more than 1,500 kilometres of driving (including a significant amount of highway) we ended up at around **14.5 kWh/100 km**. That’s seriously impressive. Even at higher speeds, the car remains efficient. And that changes everything. Fewer charging stops, lower costs, and most importantly, less stress when driving longer distances. Tesla still sets the benchmark here. ### Comfort and driving: simple, but effective Unlike the more expensive Model 3 versions, this one doesn’t get adaptive or advanced suspension systems. It keeps things simple with a more traditional setup. And yet, it works. The ride is slightly firmer over rougher surfaces, but never uncomfortable. The 18-inch wheels help absorb imperfections, and overall the car feels composed and stable. It’s not trying to be sporty, but it’s not boring either. The rear-wheel drive gives it just enough character to make it enjoyable on a twisty road, without ever becoming demanding. Exactly what most people actually want. ### Everyday usability: still one of the best As a daily car, the Model 3 continues to make a strong case for itself. The seating position works well, even for taller drivers. Rear passengers have enough space, and the combination of rear trunk and front storage makes it more practical than you might expect from a sedan. It’s not trying to be an SUV and that’s part of its strength. It stays efficient, low, and well balanced. Tesla’s biggest advantage isn’t just the tech itself, it’s how easy it is to use. Everything feels immediate and logical. Navigation is fast, settings are easy to access, and even small things (like disabling warning sounds) can be done in seconds. Where other brands often overcomplicate things, Tesla simplifies them. And that makes a huge difference in daily use. ### Price: the real game changer At €36,990, the Model 3 RWD sits in a space where competition becomes difficult. Because when you combine: efficiency, range, technology and overall usability, there’s simply not much that matches it at this price point. And that’s what makes it so strong. ### AutoNext Verdict The Tesla Model 3 RWD (2026) isn’t the most exciting electric car. It’s not the fastest, not the most luxurious, and not the most emotional. But it might be the smartest. It focuses on what actually matters and executes it exceptionally well. The efficiency is outstanding, the range is realistic, the build quality has improved, and the technology remains one of the easiest to live with. Yes, there are compromises. The lack of physical controls, the absence of CarPlay, the more basic equipment level, you notice them. But they fade quickly once you start living with the car. Because the bigger picture is simply too strong. **For this price, this might be the best all-round electric car you can buy today.** ![Mercedes-Benz EQB 250](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fa.storyblok.com%2Ff%2F286419086467324%2F6912x4608%2F47cbc1c3f1%2Fset1cjw03263.webp&w=1920&q=75)7,7/10 Avis 01/12/2025 ### Mercedes-Benz EQB 250 Twenty or so years ago, the battery electric vehicle (BEV) arms race began with exotic vehicles of all sorts, cars like the Tesla Roadster or the more recent Jaguar I-Pace. But thankfully, the world is now being fed regular models powered by batteries too, and today's subject is one of those: the Mercedes EQB 250 Luxury Line. When the Skoda Enyaq launched, it proved that this philosophy could also work in the electric era. Now Skoda takes the next step with the **all-new Skoda Elroq**, a compact electric SUV positioned below the Enyaq in the lineup. Smaller, more city-friendly and slightly more affordable, but still built on the same advanced Volkswagen Group MEB platform. [Lire l'article complet](/fr/reviews/skoda/2025-skoda-elroq-85-corporate) ![2026 BYD Seal](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fres.cloudinary.com%2Fdzmtsqtky%2Fimage%2Fupload%2Fv1774123415%2FFAT-ICE-Retromobile-2026-185_resultaat_ditjrl.webp&w=1920&q=75)6,7/10 Avis 21/03/2026 ### 2026 BYD Seal Some cars only reveal their true character when you put them through far too many kilometres in far too little time. Instead, they refined it and that shows. The front end is cleaner and sharper, the lighting slimmer, and the overall design feels more mature than before. It’s still unmistakably a Model 3, but one that has grown up. Less playful, more confident. The RWD version keeps things simple. You get 18-inch aero wheels, a limited selection of exterior colours and no unnecessary visual drama. And honestly, that suits the car perfectly. This was never meant to be a show-off, it’s designed to be efficient, and that philosophy carries through every detail. ### Interior: minimalism, but usable Inside, Tesla continues to do its own thing. Everything is controlled via the central screen. Seats, mirrors, climate settings, it all lives in the interface. At first, that’s not ideal. Adjusting your seat through a touchscreen will never be better than a physical button. But once everything is set, you quickly stop thinking about it. What stands out is how well the system works. It’s fast, logical, and incredibly easy to navigate. Compared to many competitors (especially newer brands trying to impress with endless menus) Tesla keeps things simple. You find what you need almost instantly. There’s no Apple CarPlay, which feels like a miss in the beginning. But Tesla’s own system is so well integrated that after a short time, you stop missing it altogether. ### Build quality: better than expected Tesla hasn’t always had the best reputation when it comes to build quality. Panel gaps, rattles, inconsistent finishes, we’ve all heard the stories. But this Model 3 tells a different story. Everything feels solid. Materials are well assembled, nothing squeaks, nothing feels unfinished. It’s a noticeable step forward, and one that removes a lot of the hesitation people used to have about Tesla. It simply feels like a well-built car now. And that matters. ### Performance: exactly what you need On paper, the numbers are modest compared to the higher-end versions. Around 283 horsepower and 420 Nm of torque. In reality, it’s more than enough. Acceleration is instant, smooth, and perfectly usable in daily driving. It doesn’t try to overwhelm you, but it never feels slow either. The rear-wheel-drive setup adds a layer of balance that makes the car feel natural and predictable. This isn’t about chasing performance figures. It’s about delivering just the right amount of power, exactly when you need it. ### Efficiency: this is where it wins If there’s one area where the Model 3 RWD truly stands out, it’s efficiency. Tesla claims a WLTP range of just over 500 kilometres with a consumption figure around 13 to 14 kWh per 100 kilometres. Normally, you take those numbers with a grain of salt. Here, you don’t have to. Over more than 1,500 kilometres of driving (including a significant amount of highway) we ended up at around **14.5 kWh/100 km**. That’s seriously impressive. Even at higher speeds, the car remains efficient. And that changes everything. Fewer charging stops, lower costs, and most importantly, less stress when driving longer distances. Tesla still sets the benchmark here. ### Comfort and driving: simple, but effective Unlike the more expensive Model 3 versions, this one doesn’t get adaptive or advanced suspension systems. It keeps things simple with a more traditional setup. And yet, it works. The ride is slightly firmer over rougher surfaces, but never uncomfortable. The 18-inch wheels help absorb imperfections, and overall the car feels composed and stable. It’s not trying to be sporty, but it’s not boring either. The rear-wheel drive gives it just enough character to make it enjoyable on a twisty road, without ever becoming demanding. Exactly what most people actually want. ### Everyday usability: still one of the best As a daily car, the Model 3 continues to make a strong case for itself. The seating position works well, even for taller drivers. Rear passengers have enough space, and the combination of rear trunk and front storage makes it more practical than you might expect from a sedan. It’s not trying to be an SUV and that’s part of its strength. It stays efficient, low, and well balanced. Tesla’s biggest advantage isn’t just the tech itself, it’s how easy it is to use. Everything feels immediate and logical. Navigation is fast, settings are easy to access, and even small things (like disabling warning sounds) can be done in seconds. Where other brands often overcomplicate things, Tesla simplifies them. And that makes a huge difference in daily use. ### Price: the real game changer At €36,990, the Model 3 RWD sits in a space where competition becomes difficult. Because when you combine: efficiency, range, technology and overall usability, there’s simply not much that matches it at this price point. And that’s what makes it so strong. ### AutoNext Verdict The Tesla Model 3 RWD (2026) isn’t the most exciting electric car. It’s not the fastest, not the most luxurious, and not the most emotional. But it might be the smartest. It focuses on what actually matters and executes it exceptionally well. The efficiency is outstanding, the range is realistic, the build quality has improved, and the technology remains one of the easiest to live with. Yes, there are compromises. The lack of physical controls, the absence of CarPlay, the more basic equipment level, you notice them. But they fade quickly once you start living with the car. Because the bigger picture is simply too strong. **For this price, this might be the best all-round electric car you can buy today.** ![Mercedes-Benz EQB 250](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fa.storyblok.com%2Ff%2F286419086467324%2F6912x4608%2F47cbc1c3f1%2Fset1cjw03263.webp&w=1920&q=75)7,7/10 Avis 01/12/2025 ### Mercedes-Benz EQB 250 Twenty or so years ago, the battery electric vehicle (BEV) arms race began with exotic vehicles of all sorts, cars like the Tesla Roadster or the more recent Jaguar I-Pace. But thankfully, the world is now being fed regular models powered by batteries too, and today's subject is one of those: the Mercedes EQB 250 Luxury Line. Less power than the Performance versions, fewer features, a simpler setup and yet, after spending serious time with it, one conclusion keeps coming back: This might be the most rational electric car you can buy right now. Starting at just **€36,990**, it undercuts a large part of the competition. But what makes it interesting isn’t just the price, it’s how little you feel like you’re missing. ### Design: evolution done right With the Highland update, Tesla didn’t try to reinvent the Model 3. Instead, they refined it and that shows. The front end is cleaner and sharper, the lighting slimmer, and the overall design feels more mature than before. It’s still unmistakably a Model 3, but one that has grown up. Less playful, more confident. The RWD version keeps things simple. You get 18-inch aero wheels, a limited selection of exterior colours and no unnecessary visual drama. And honestly, that suits the car perfectly. This was never meant to be a show-off, it’s designed to be efficient, and that philosophy carries through every detail. ### Interior: minimalism, but usable Inside, Tesla continues to do its own thing. Everything is controlled via the central screen. Seats, mirrors, climate settings, it all lives in the interface. At first, that’s not ideal. Adjusting your seat through a touchscreen will never be better than a physical button. But once everything is set, you quickly stop thinking about it. What stands out is how well the system works. It’s fast, logical, and incredibly easy to navigate. Compared to many competitors (especially newer brands trying to impress with endless menus) Tesla keeps things simple. You find what you need almost instantly. There’s no Apple CarPlay, which feels like a miss in the beginning. But Tesla’s own system is so well integrated that after a short time, you stop missing it altogether. ### Build quality: better than expected Tesla hasn’t always had the best reputation when it comes to build quality. Panel gaps, rattles, inconsistent finishes, we’ve all heard the stories. But this Model 3 tells a different story. Everything feels solid. Materials are well assembled, nothing squeaks, nothing feels unfinished. It’s a noticeable step forward, and one that removes a lot of the hesitation people used to have about Tesla. It simply feels like a well-built car now. And that matters. ### Performance: exactly what you need On paper, the numbers are modest compared to the higher-end versions. Around 283 horsepower and 420 Nm of torque. In reality, it’s more than enough. Acceleration is instant, smooth, and perfectly usable in daily driving. It doesn’t try to overwhelm you, but it never feels slow either. The rear-wheel-drive setup adds a layer of balance that makes the car feel natural and predictable. This isn’t about chasing performance figures. It’s about delivering just the right amount of power, exactly when you need it. ### Efficiency: this is where it wins If there’s one area where the Model 3 RWD truly stands out, it’s efficiency. Tesla claims a WLTP range of just over 500 kilometres with a consumption figure around 13 to 14 kWh per 100 kilometres. Normally, you take those numbers with a grain of salt. Here, you don’t have to. Over more than 1,500 kilometres of driving (including a significant amount of highway) we ended up at around **14.5 kWh/100 km**. That’s seriously impressive. Even at higher speeds, the car remains efficient. And that changes everything. Fewer charging stops, lower costs, and most importantly, less stress when driving longer distances. Tesla still sets the benchmark here. ### Comfort and driving: simple, but effective Unlike the more expensive Model 3 versions, this one doesn’t get adaptive or advanced suspension systems. It keeps things simple with a more traditional setup. And yet, it works. The ride is slightly firmer over rougher surfaces, but never uncomfortable. The 18-inch wheels help absorb imperfections, and overall the car feels composed and stable. It’s not trying to be sporty, but it’s not boring either. The rear-wheel drive gives it just enough character to make it enjoyable on a twisty road, without ever becoming demanding. Exactly what most people actually want. ### Everyday usability: still one of the best As a daily car, the Model 3 continues to make a strong case for itself. The seating position works well, even for taller drivers. Rear passengers have enough space, and the combination of rear trunk and front storage makes it more practical than you might expect from a sedan. It’s not trying to be an SUV and that’s part of its strength. It stays efficient, low, and well balanced. Tesla’s biggest advantage isn’t just the tech itself, it’s how easy it is to use. Everything feels immediate and logical. Navigation is fast, settings are easy to access, and even small things (like disabling warning sounds) can be done in seconds. Where other brands often overcomplicate things, Tesla simplifies them. And that makes a huge difference in daily use. ### Price: the real game changer At €36,990, the Model 3 RWD sits in a space where competition becomes difficult. Because when you combine: efficiency, range, technology and overall usability, there’s simply not much that matches it at this price point. And that’s what makes it so strong. ### AutoNext Verdict The Tesla Model 3 RWD (2026) isn’t the most exciting electric car. It’s not the fastest, not the most luxurious, and not the most emotional. But it might be the smartest. It focuses on what actually matters and executes it exceptionally well. The efficiency is outstanding, the range is realistic, the build quality has improved, and the technology remains one of the easiest to live with. Yes, there are compromises. The lack of physical controls, the absence of CarPlay, the more basic equipment level, you notice them. But they fade quickly once you start living with the car. It’s not trying to be an SUV and that’s part of its strength. It stays efficient, low, and well balanced. Tesla’s biggest advantage isn’t just the tech itself, it’s how easy it is to use. Everything feels immediate and logical. Navigation is fast, settings are easy to access, and even small things (like disabling warning sounds) can be done in seconds. Adjusting your seat through a touchscreen will never be better than a physical button. But once everything is set, you quickly stop thinking about it. What stands out is how well the system works. It’s fast, logical, and incredibly easy to navigate. Compared to many competitors (especially newer brands trying to impress with endless menus) Tesla keeps things simple. You find what you need almost instantly. There’s no Apple CarPlay, which feels like a miss in the beginning. But Tesla’s own system is so well integrated that after a short time, you stop missing it altogether. ### Build quality: better than expected Tesla hasn’t always had the best reputation when it comes to build quality. Panel gaps, rattles, inconsistent finishes, we’ve all heard the stories. But this Model 3 tells a different story. Everything feels solid. Materials are well assembled, nothing squeaks, nothing feels unfinished. It’s a noticeable step forward, and one that removes a lot of the hesitation people used to have about Tesla. It simply feels like a well-built car now. And that matters. ### Performance: exactly what you need On paper, the numbers are modest compared to the higher-end versions. Around 283 horsepower and 420 Nm of torque. In reality, it’s more than enough. Acceleration is instant, smooth, and perfectly usable in daily driving. It doesn’t try to overwhelm you, but it never feels slow either. The rear-wheel-drive setup adds a layer of balance that makes the car feel natural and predictable. This isn’t about chasing performance figures. It’s about delivering just the right amount of power, exactly when you need it. ### Efficiency: this is where it wins If there’s one area where the Model 3 RWD truly stands out, it’s efficiency. Tesla claims a WLTP range of just over 500 kilometres with a consumption figure around 13 to 14 kWh per 100 kilometres. Normally, you take those numbers with a grain of salt. Here, you don’t have to. Over more than 1,500 kilometres of driving (including a significant amount of highway) we ended up at around **14.5 kWh/100 km**. That’s seriously impressive. Even at higher speeds, the car remains efficient. And that changes everything. Fewer charging stops, lower costs, and most importantly, less stress when driving longer distances. Tesla still sets the benchmark here. ### Comfort and driving: simple, but effective Unlike the more expensive Model 3 versions, this one doesn’t get adaptive or advanced suspension systems. It keeps things simple with a more traditional setup. And yet, it works. The ride is slightly firmer over rougher surfaces, but never uncomfortable. The 18-inch wheels help absorb imperfections, and overall the car feels composed and stable. It’s not trying to be sporty, but it’s not boring either. The rear-wheel drive gives it just enough character to make it enjoyable on a twisty road, without ever becoming demanding. Exactly what most people actually want. ### Everyday usability: still one of the best As a daily car, the Model 3 continues to make a strong case for itself. The seating position works well, even for taller drivers. Rear passengers have enough space, and the combination of rear trunk and front storage makes it more practical than you might expect from a sedan. It’s not trying to be an SUV and that’s part of its strength. It stays efficient, low, and well balanced. Tesla’s biggest advantage isn’t just the tech itself, it’s how easy it is to use. Everything feels immediate and logical. Navigation is fast, settings are easy to access, and even small things (like disabling warning sounds) can be done in seconds. Where other brands often overcomplicate things, Tesla simplifies them. And that makes a huge difference in daily use. ### Price: the real game changer At €36,990, the Model 3 RWD sits in a space where competition becomes difficult. Because when you combine: efficiency, range, technology and overall usability, there’s simply not much that matches it at this price point. And that’s what makes it so strong. ### AutoNext Verdict The Tesla Model 3 RWD (2026) isn’t the most exciting electric car. It’s not the fastest, not the most luxurious, and not the most emotional. But it might be the smartest. It focuses on what actually matters and executes it exceptionally well. The efficiency is outstanding, the range is realistic, the build quality has improved, and the technology remains one of the easiest to live with. Yes, there are compromises. The lack of physical controls, the absence of CarPlay, the more basic equipment level, you notice them. But they fade quickly once you start living with the car. Because the bigger picture is simply too strong. **For this price, this might be the best all-round electric car you can buy today.** ![Mercedes-Benz EQB 250](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fa.storyblok.com%2Ff%2F286419086467324%2F6912x4608%2F47cbc1c3f1%2Fset1cjw03263.webp&w=1920&q=75)7,7/10 Avis 01/12/2025 ### Mercedes-Benz EQB 250 Twenty or so years ago, the battery electric vehicle (BEV) arms race began with exotic vehicles of all sorts, cars like the Tesla Roadster or the more recent Jaguar I-Pace. But thankfully, the world is now being fed regular models powered by batteries too, and today's subject is one of those: the Mercedes EQB 250 Luxury Line. Oxford Economics findings say 26% of the growth in Jacksonville’s gross domestic product in 2025 can be attributed to the technology sector. It specifically cited the presence of Financial Technology firms like Fidelity National Information Services, Nymbus and Black Knight, as well as large presence from traditional banks like Bank of America, TIAA, Wells Fargo, BBVA and Truist. That’s based on the regional population of 1.8 million, while Jacksonville proper/Duval County is about 1.1 million people. The firm weighs the strength of a city’s economics, human capital, quality of life, environment and governance to compile the ranking. The report puts Jacksonville 134th overall out of the 1,000 cities ranked in the study. The Northeast Florida city was in the top five to watch in North America with Boise, Idaho; Durham, North Carolina; San Antonio, Texas; and Edmonton in Alberta, Canada. Oxford Economics findings say 26% of the growth in Jacksonville’s gross domestic product in 2025 can be attributed to the technology sector. It specifically cited the presence of Financial Technology firms like Fidelity National Information Services, Nymbus and Black Knight, as well as large presence from traditional banks like Bank of America, TIAA, Wells Fargo, BBVA and Truist. The city’s total GDP is $148 billion, according to Oxford Economics, or $83,200 per person. That’s based on the regional population of 1.8 million, while Jacksonville proper/Duval County is about 1.1 million people. The Oxford index forecasts a 1% population growth rate per year through 2030, nearly four times the U.S. rate. It highlights the city’s high income per person, smaller rainfall anomalies and large GDP size as strengths. trunks.title: Jacksonville's Culinary Rise: Why It's a Top 5 City for World-Class Ingredients
trunks.script: Jacksonville has emerged as a top city for world-class ingredients, thanks to its vibrant arts and culture scene. The city offers a rich array of culinary experiences through its diverse food and drink offerings. Visitors can explore local markets, restaurants, and events that highlight the region's agricultural bounty and innovative chefs. Jacksonville's commitment to supporting local farmers and producers ensures a steady supply of fresh, high-quality ingredients for its culinary scene.
