Jacksonville’s city and business leaders held a news conference Tuesday at City Hall to celebrate the city’s position on the index and reaffirm their goal to make Jacksonville a top 50 city globally by 2032. Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Mayor Donna Deegan says the city’s improving economic metrics noted in Oxford’s recognition are “not a partisan issue.” The Democratic mayor was joined at the news conference by City Council President Nick Howland, a Republican; Jacksonville Civic Council President and CEO Dennis Whittle; and Daniel Davis, Jax Chamber president and CEO and Deegan’s opponent in the 2023 mayoral election. “Just last week, we opened the UF Jacksonville campus, and we were recognized for having the fastest-growing workforce in the country,” Deegan said. “We already know what’s happening in this city — the investment, the growth, the opportunity we’re building in Downtown and every neighborhood. It’s wonderful to see the rest of the world beginning to recognize it too.” [Article continues below](#most-read-ad-unit) #### More from Jax Today [## Pediatric illnesses illuminate hunger challenge facing Northeast Florida families](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/northeast-florida-childhood-hunger/)[## Second case of West Nile Virus found in Duval County](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/west-nile-virus-duval/)[## St. Johns County reverses course and denies 4,000-home development near Nocatee](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/st-johns-rejects-enclave-development/) Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Oxford Economics’ index currently ranks Jacksonville 97th globally for cities with a population of 4 million or less, a bump from its 119th position on the index last year. The firm weighs the strength of a city’s economics, human capital, quality of life, environment and governance to compile the ranking. The report puts Jacksonville 134th overall out of the 1,000 cities ranked in the study. The Northeast Florida city was in the top five to watch in North America with Boise, Idaho; Durham, North Carolina; San Antonio, Texas; and Edmonton in Alberta, Canada. Oxford Economics findings say 26% of the growth in Jacksonville’s gross domestic product in 2025 can be attributed to the technology sector. It specifically cited the presence of Financial Technology firms like Fidelity National Information Services, Nymbus and Black Knight, as well as large presence from traditional banks like Bank of America, TIAA, Wells Fargo, BBVA and Truist. The city’s total GDP is $148 billion, according to Oxford Economics, or $83,200 per person. That’s based on the regional population of 1.8 million, while Jacksonville proper/Duval County is about 1.1 million people. The Oxford index forecasts a 1% population growth rate per year through 2030, nearly four times the U.S. rate. It highlights the city’s high income per person, smaller rainfall anomalies and large GDP size as strengths. Weaknesses include Jacksonville’s higher crime rate, higher housing expenditures and older age profile. “Jacksonville is a standout city — even by fast-growing Florida standards,” the report states. “Its broad-based growth in recent years has earned it an upgrade in the Global City Index rankings for this year. While much of its growth has been fueled by in-migration and population gains, it is increasingly being recognized on a global scale for its burgeoning finance, tech, fintech, and professional business services sectors.” [Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf)[Download](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf) Howland credited Florida and Jacksonville’s low taxes, relative to Northeastern, Midwestern and Florida peer cities. He also says the city is more “recession proof” with a large share of its jobs in the military, logistics, medical and manufacturing sectors. “We are a low-tax environment. Families and businesses can keep more of the hard-earned money that they make than nearly everywhere else in America,” Howland said. “It’s our quality of life. Our climate, our beach, our rivers — you heard it said — our waterways, our growing culinary scene, our improving Downtown and riverfront, and our improving NFL team. We’re investing in all the right places.” ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-and-Howland-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Mayor Donna Deegan and City Council President Nick Howland attend a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Deegan has been critical of the state Legislature’s push to persuade voters to approve a constitutional amendment to drastically scale back residential property taxes. She said the ranking should be a call for more public-private partnerships and more public and private sector investments in the city’s quality of life to maintain momentum. “It calls for us to attract new people while making sure that the families who built this city can afford to remain here and share in its success,” Deegan said. ### Economic headwinds and Amendment 3 Many of the data points for the ranking were taken from Jacksonville’s 2025 economic numbers. Today, there are some signs that job growth in Northeast Florida could be slowing. The state’s Department of Commerce reported last month that Northeast Florida’s [rate of job growth slowed](https://www.jaxdailyrecord.com/news/2026/aug/24/unemployment-rate-rises-to-49-in-northeast-florida/) in July, and the unemployment rate ticked up from 4.8% in June to 4.9%. The Jacksonville metropolitan area saw 2,900 nonfarm jobs added from July 2025 to July 2026, a 0.4% growth rate. There’s also worry about less property tax revenue for public sector spending by the city if Amendment 3 passes in November. The Jacksonville City Council auditor estimates the Florida property tax cut would mean $300 million less per year for the city by 2027. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Dennis-Whittle-at-Oxford-presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Civic Council CEO Dennis Whittle speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Whittle said when he came to Jacksonville seven years ago, he saw the city’s “world-class ingredients.” The Civic Council CEO says the organization, a panel of 100 of the region’s business executives, will meet to consider a position on the tax referendum soon. He declined to comment directly Tuesday about the tax cut before his board meets. “A lot of people have spoken out against the amendment — the [police and fire unions and a number of sheriffs](https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2026/09/15/florida-sheriffs-firefighters-slam-property-tax-amendment-as-a-train-wreck/). I won’t repeat what they’ve said,” Whittle said. “But I would hate for us to do anything that took the wind out of the sails of what you’re seeing here today,” Whittle said. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Daniel-Davis-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jax Chamber President and CEO Daniel Davis speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Davis touted job creation at [Cecil Airport and Spaceport](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/08/31/fscj-cecil-spaceport-jobs-training/) and the growing commerce center that surrounds it, as integral to making Oxford Economics’ forecast for Jacksonville a reality. Howland has also made attracting more aerospace businesses to Cecil to join companies like Boeing and Otto Aerospace a priority of his council presidency. “We will be a top 50 city, mark my words,” Davis said. “It only happens when all get behind what the mayor’s doing. When we all get behind the leadership of growing jobs at Cecil with City Council President Howland. trunks.title: Jacksonville's Culinary Rise: Why It's a Top 5 City for World-Class Ingredients
trunks.script: Jacksonville has seen a significant culinary transformation, becoming a top 5 city for world-class ingredients. The city's climate and geography contribute to its rich agricultural diversity, supporting local farmers and suppliers. This abundance of fresh, high-quality produce and proteins has attracted top chefs and restaurants, enhancing the dining experience for locals and visitors alike.

Jacksonville’s city and business leaders held a news conference Tuesday at City Hall to celebrate the city’s position on the index and reaffirm their goal to make Jacksonville a top 50 city globally by 2032. Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Mayor Donna Deegan says the city’s improving economic metrics noted in Oxford’s recognition are “not a partisan issue.” The Democratic mayor was joined at the news conference by City Council President Nick Howland, a Republican; Jacksonville Civic Council President and CEO Dennis Whittle; and Daniel Davis, Jax Chamber president and CEO and Deegan’s opponent in the 2023 mayoral election. “Just last week, we opened the UF Jacksonville campus, and we were recognized for having the fastest-growing workforce in the country,” Deegan said. “We already know what’s happening in this city — the investment, the growth, the opportunity we’re building in Downtown and every neighborhood. It’s wonderful to see the rest of the world beginning to recognize it too.” [Article continues below](#most-read-ad-unit) #### More from Jax Today [## Pediatric illnesses illuminate hunger challenge facing Northeast Florida families](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/northeast-florida-childhood-hunger/)[## Second case of West Nile Virus found in Duval County](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/west-nile-virus-duval/)[## St. Johns County reverses course and denies 4,000-home development near Nocatee](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/st-johns-rejects-enclave-development/) Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Oxford Economics’ index currently ranks Jacksonville 97th globally for cities with a population of 4 million or less, a bump from its 119th position on the index last year. The firm weighs the strength of a city’s economics, human capital, quality of life, environment and governance to compile the ranking. The report puts Jacksonville 134th overall out of the 1,000 cities ranked in the study. The Northeast Florida city was in the top five to watch in North America with Boise, Idaho; Durham, North Carolina; San Antonio, Texas; and Edmonton in Alberta, Canada. Oxford Economics findings say 26% of the growth in Jacksonville’s gross domestic product in 2025 can be attributed to the technology sector. It specifically cited the presence of Financial Technology firms like Fidelity National Information Services, Nymbus and Black Knight, as well as large presence from traditional banks like Bank of America, TIAA, Wells Fargo, BBVA and Truist. The city’s total GDP is $148 billion, according to Oxford Economics, or $83,200 per person. That’s based on the regional population of 1.8 million, while Jacksonville proper/Duval County is about 1.1 million people. The Oxford index forecasts a 1% population growth rate per year through 2030, nearly four times the U.S. rate. It highlights the city’s high income per person, smaller rainfall anomalies and large GDP size as strengths. Weaknesses include Jacksonville’s higher crime rate, higher housing expenditures and older age profile. “Jacksonville is a standout city — even by fast-growing Florida standards,” the report states. “Its broad-based growth in recent years has earned it an upgrade in the Global City Index rankings for this year. While much of its growth has been fueled by in-migration and population gains, it is increasingly being recognized on a global scale for its burgeoning finance, tech, fintech, and professional business services sectors.” [Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf)[Download](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf) Howland credited Florida and Jacksonville’s low taxes, relative to Northeastern, Midwestern and Florida peer cities. He also says the city is more “recession proof” with a large share of its jobs in the military, logistics, medical and manufacturing sectors. “We are a low-tax environment. Families and businesses can keep more of the hard-earned money that they make than nearly everywhere else in America,” Howland said. “It’s our quality of life. Our climate, our beach, our rivers — you heard it said — our waterways, our growing culinary scene, our improving Downtown and riverfront, and our improving NFL team. We’re investing in all the right places.” ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-and-Howland-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Mayor Donna Deegan and City Council President Nick Howland attend a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Deegan has been critical of the state Legislature’s push to persuade voters to approve a constitutional amendment to drastically scale back residential property taxes. She said the ranking should be a call for more public-private partnerships and more public and private sector investments in the city’s quality of life to maintain momentum. “It calls for us to attract new people while making sure that the families who built this city can afford to remain here and share in its success,” Deegan said. ### Economic headwinds and Amendment 3 Many of the data points for the ranking were taken from Jacksonville’s 2025 economic numbers. Today, there are some signs that job growth in Northeast Florida could be slowing. The state’s Department of Commerce reported last month that Northeast Florida’s [rate of job growth slowed](https://www.jaxdailyrecord.com/news/2026/aug/24/unemployment-rate-rises-to-49-in-northeast-florida/) in July, and the unemployment rate ticked up from 4.8% in June to 4.9%. The Jacksonville metropolitan area saw 2,900 nonfarm jobs added from July 2025 to July 2026, a 0.4% growth rate. There’s also worry about less property tax revenue for public sector spending by the city if Amendment 3 passes in November. The Jacksonville City Council auditor estimates the Florida property tax cut would mean $300 million less per year for the city by 2027. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Dennis-Whittle-at-Oxford-presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Civic Council CEO Dennis Whittle speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Whittle said when he came to Jacksonville seven years ago, he saw the city’s “world-class ingredients.” The Civic Council CEO says the organization, a panel of 100 of the region’s business executives, will meet to consider a position on the tax referendum soon. He declined to comment directly Tuesday about the tax cut before his board meets. “A lot of people have spoken out against the amendment — the [police and fire unions and a number of sheriffs](https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2026/09/15/florida-sheriffs-firefighters-slam-property-tax-amendment-as-a-train-wreck/). I won’t repeat what they’ve said,” Whittle said. “But I would hate for us to do anything that took the wind out of the sails of what you’re seeing here today,” Whittle said. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Daniel-Davis-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jax Chamber President and CEO Daniel Davis speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Davis touted job creation at [Cecil Airport and Spaceport](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/08/31/fscj-cecil-spaceport-jobs-training/) and the growing commerce center that surrounds it, as integral to making Oxford Economics’ forecast for Jacksonville a reality. Howland has also made attracting more aerospace businesses to Cecil to join companies like Boeing and Otto Aerospace a priority of his council presidency. “We will be a top 50 city, mark my words,” Davis said. “It only happens when all get behind what the mayor’s doing. When we all get behind the leadership of growing jobs at Cecil with City Council President Howland. trunks.title: Jacksonville's Culinary Rise: Why It's a Top 5 City for World-Class Ingredients
trunks.script: Jacksonville has emerged as a top city for world-class ingredients, thanks to its vibrant culinary scene. The city's commitment to affordable housing and community support has attracted talented chefs and local farmers, enhancing the quality and variety of local produce. Initiatives like the Dinner Club further promote culinary excellence, bringing together local talent and food enthusiasts to celebrate Jacksonville's rich food culture.

Jacksonville’s city and business leaders held a news conference Tuesday at City Hall to celebrate the city’s position on the index and reaffirm their goal to make Jacksonville a top 50 city globally by 2032. Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Mayor Donna Deegan says the city’s improving economic metrics noted in Oxford’s recognition are “not a partisan issue.” The Democratic mayor was joined at the news conference by City Council President Nick Howland, a Republican; Jacksonville Civic Council President and CEO Dennis Whittle; and Daniel Davis, Jax Chamber president and CEO and Deegan’s opponent in the 2023 mayoral election. “Just last week, we opened the UF Jacksonville campus, and we were recognized for having the fastest-growing workforce in the country,” Deegan said. “We already know what’s happening in this city — the investment, the growth, the opportunity we’re building in Downtown and every neighborhood. It’s wonderful to see the rest of the world beginning to recognize it too.” [Article continues below](#most-read-ad-unit) #### More from Jax Today [## Pediatric illnesses illuminate hunger challenge facing Northeast Florida families](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/northeast-florida-childhood-hunger/)[## Second case of West Nile Virus found in Duval County](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/west-nile-virus-duval/)[## St. Johns County reverses course and denies 4,000-home development near Nocatee](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/st-johns-rejects-enclave-development/) Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Oxford Economics’ index currently ranks Jacksonville 97th globally for cities with a population of 4 million or less, a bump from its 119th position on the index last year. The firm weighs the strength of a city’s economics, human capital, quality of life, environment and governance to compile the ranking. The report puts Jacksonville 134th overall out of the 1,000 cities ranked in the study. The Northeast Florida city was in the top five to watch in North America with Boise, Idaho; Durham, North Carolina; San Antonio, Texas; and Edmonton in Alberta, Canada. Oxford Economics findings say 26% of the growth in Jacksonville’s gross domestic product in 2025 can be attributed to the technology sector. It specifically cited the presence of Financial Technology firms like Fidelity National Information Services, Nymbus and Black Knight, as well as large presence from traditional banks like Bank of America, TIAA, Wells Fargo, BBVA and Truist. The city’s total GDP is $148 billion, according to Oxford Economics, or $83,200 per person. That’s based on the regional population of 1.8 million, while Jacksonville proper/Duval County is about 1.1 million people. The Oxford index forecasts a 1% population growth rate per year through 2030, nearly four times the U.S. rate. It highlights the city’s high income per person, smaller rainfall anomalies and large GDP size as strengths. Weaknesses include Jacksonville’s higher crime rate, higher housing expenditures and older age profile. “Jacksonville is a standout city — even by fast-growing Florida standards,” the report states. “Its broad-based growth in recent years has earned it an upgrade in the Global City Index rankings for this year. While much of its growth has been fueled by in-migration and population gains, it is increasingly being recognized on a global scale for its burgeoning finance, tech, fintech, and professional business services sectors.” [Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf)[Download](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf) Howland credited Florida and Jacksonville’s low taxes, relative to Northeastern, Midwestern and Florida peer cities. He also says the city is more “recession proof” with a large share of its jobs in the military, logistics, medical and manufacturing sectors. “We are a low-tax environment. Families and businesses can keep more of the hard-earned money that they make than nearly everywhere else in America,” Howland said. “It’s our quality of life. Our climate, our beach, our rivers — you heard it said — our waterways, our growing culinary scene, our improving Downtown and riverfront, and our improving NFL team. We’re investing in all the right places.” ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-and-Howland-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Mayor Donna Deegan and City Council President Nick Howland attend a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Deegan has been critical of the state Legislature’s push to persuade voters to approve a constitutional amendment to drastically scale back residential property taxes. She said the ranking should be a call for more public-private partnerships and more public and private sector investments in the city’s quality of life to maintain momentum. “It calls for us to attract new people while making sure that the families who built this city can afford to remain here and share in its success,” Deegan said. ### Economic headwinds and Amendment 3 Many of the data points for the ranking were taken from Jacksonville’s 2025 economic numbers. Today, there are some signs that job growth in Northeast Florida could be slowing. The state’s Department of Commerce reported last month that Northeast Florida’s [rate of job growth slowed](https://www.jaxdailyrecord.com/news/2026/aug/24/unemployment-rate-rises-to-49-in-northeast-florida/) in July, and the unemployment rate ticked up from 4.8% in June to 4.9%. The Jacksonville metropolitan area saw 2,900 nonfarm jobs added from July 2025 to July 2026, a 0.4% growth rate. There’s also worry about less property tax revenue for public sector spending by the city if Amendment 3 passes in November. The Jacksonville City Council auditor estimates the Florida property tax cut would mean $300 million less per year for the city by 2027. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Dennis-Whittle-at-Oxford-presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Civic Council CEO Dennis Whittle speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Whittle said when he came to Jacksonville seven years ago, he saw the city’s “world-class ingredients.” The Civic Council CEO says the organization, a panel of 100 of the region’s business executives, will meet to consider a position on the tax referendum soon. He declined to comment directly Tuesday about the tax cut before his board meets. “A lot of people have spoken out against the amendment — the [police and fire unions and a number of sheriffs](https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2026/09/15/florida-sheriffs-firefighters-slam-property-tax-amendment-as-a-train-wreck/). I won’t repeat what they’ve said,” Whittle said. “But I would hate for us to do anything that took the wind out of the sails of what you’re seeing here today,” Whittle said. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Daniel-Davis-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jax Chamber President and CEO Daniel Davis speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Davis touted job creation at [Cecil Airport and Spaceport](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/08/31/fscj-cecil-spaceport-jobs-training/) and the growing commerce center that surrounds it, as integral to making Oxford Economics’ forecast for Jacksonville a reality. Howland has also made attracting more aerospace businesses to Cecil to join companies like Boeing and Otto Aerospace a priority of his council presidency. “We will be a top 50 city, mark my words,” Davis said. “It only happens when all get behind what the mayor’s doing. When we all get behind the leadership of growing jobs at Cecil with City Council President Howland. trunks.title: Jacksonville's Culinary Rise: Why It's a Top 5 City for World-Class Ingredients
trunks.script: Jacksonville has emerged as a top city for world-class ingredients, thanks to its strategic location and commitment to culinary excellence. The city's proximity to the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean provides access to fresh seafood, while its inland waterways offer a variety of freshwater fish. Local farmers and producers also contribute to the city's vibrant food scene, ensuring a diverse array of locally sourced ingredients. This combination of fresh, locally sourced products and innovative culinary practices has positioned Jacksonville as a must-visit destination for food enthusiasts.

Jacksonville’s city and business leaders held a news conference Tuesday at City Hall to celebrate the city’s position on the index and reaffirm their goal to make Jacksonville a top 50 city globally by 2032. Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Mayor Donna Deegan says the city’s improving economic metrics noted in Oxford’s recognition are “not a partisan issue.” The Democratic mayor was joined at the news conference by City Council President Nick Howland, a Republican; Jacksonville Civic Council President and CEO Dennis Whittle; and Daniel Davis, Jax Chamber president and CEO and Deegan’s opponent in the 2023 mayoral election. “Just last week, we opened the UF Jacksonville campus, and we were recognized for having the fastest-growing workforce in the country,” Deegan said. “We already know what’s happening in this city — the investment, the growth, the opportunity we’re building in Downtown and every neighborhood. It’s wonderful to see the rest of the world beginning to recognize it too.” [Article continues below](#most-read-ad-unit) #### More from Jax Today [## Pediatric illnesses illuminate hunger challenge facing Northeast Florida families](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/northeast-florida-childhood-hunger/)[## Second case of West Nile Virus found in Duval County](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/west-nile-virus-duval/)[## St. Johns County reverses course and denies 4,000-home development near Nocatee](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/st-johns-rejects-enclave-development/) Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Oxford Economics’ index currently ranks Jacksonville 97th globally for cities with a population of 4 million or less, a bump from its 119th position on the index last year. The firm weighs the strength of a city’s economics, human capital, quality of life, environment and governance to compile the ranking. The report puts Jacksonville 134th overall out of the 1,000 cities ranked in the study. The Northeast Florida city was in the top five to watch in North America with Boise, Idaho; Durham, North Carolina; San Antonio, Texas; and Edmonton in Alberta, Canada. Oxford Economics findings say 26% of the growth in Jacksonville’s gross domestic product in 2025 can be attributed to the technology sector. It specifically cited the presence of Financial Technology firms like Fidelity National Information Services, Nymbus and Black Knight, as well as large presence from traditional banks like Bank of America, TIAA, Wells Fargo, BBVA and Truist. The city’s total GDP is $148 billion, according to Oxford Economics, or $83,200 per person. That’s based on the regional population of 1.8 million, while Jacksonville proper/Duval County is about 1.1 million people. The Oxford index forecasts a 1% population growth rate per year through 2030, nearly four times the U.S. rate. It highlights the city’s high income per person, smaller rainfall anomalies and large GDP size as strengths. Weaknesses include Jacksonville’s higher crime rate, higher housing expenditures and older age profile. “Jacksonville is a standout city — even by fast-growing Florida standards,” the report states. “Its broad-based growth in recent years has earned it an upgrade in the Global City Index rankings for this year. While much of its growth has been fueled by in-migration and population gains, it is increasingly being recognized on a global scale for its burgeoning finance, tech, fintech, and professional business services sectors.” [Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf)[Download](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf) Howland credited Florida and Jacksonville’s low taxes, relative to Northeastern, Midwestern and Florida peer cities. He also says the city is more “recession proof” with a large share of its jobs in the military, logistics, medical and manufacturing sectors. “We are a low-tax environment. Families and businesses can keep more of the hard-earned money that they make than nearly everywhere else in America,” Howland said. “It’s our quality of life. Our climate, our beach, our rivers — you heard it said — our waterways, our growing culinary scene, our improving Downtown and riverfront, and our improving NFL team. We’re investing in all the right places.” ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-and-Howland-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Mayor Donna Deegan and City Council President Nick Howland attend a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Deegan has been critical of the state Legislature’s push to persuade voters to approve a constitutional amendment to drastically scale back residential property taxes. She said the ranking should be a call for more public-private partnerships and more public and private sector investments in the city’s quality of life to maintain momentum. “It calls for us to attract new people while making sure that the families who built this city can afford to remain here and share in its success,” Deegan said. ### Economic headwinds and Amendment 3 Many of the data points for the ranking were taken from Jacksonville’s 2025 economic numbers. Today, there are some signs that job growth in Northeast Florida could be slowing. The state’s Department of Commerce reported last month that Northeast Florida’s [rate of job growth slowed](https://www.jaxdailyrecord.com/news/2026/aug/24/unemployment-rate-rises-to-49-in-northeast-florida/) in July, and the unemployment rate ticked up from 4.8% in June to 4.9%. The Jacksonville metropolitan area saw 2,900 nonfarm jobs added from July 2025 to July 2026, a 0.4% growth rate. There’s also worry about less property tax revenue for public sector spending by the city if Amendment 3 passes in November. The Jacksonville City Council auditor estimates the Florida property tax cut would mean $300 million less per year for the city by 2027. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Dennis-Whittle-at-Oxford-presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Civic Council CEO Dennis Whittle speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Whittle said when he came to Jacksonville seven years ago, he saw the city’s “world-class ingredients.” The Civic Council CEO says the organization, a panel of 100 of the region’s business executives, will meet to consider a position on the tax referendum soon. He declined to comment directly Tuesday about the tax cut before his board meets. “A lot of people have spoken out against the amendment — the [police and fire unions and a number of sheriffs](https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2026/09/15/florida-sheriffs-firefighters-slam-property-tax-amendment-as-a-train-wreck/). I won’t repeat what they’ve said,” Whittle said. “But I would hate for us to do anything that took the wind out of the sails of what you’re seeing here today,” Whittle said. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Daniel-Davis-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jax Chamber President and CEO Daniel Davis speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Davis touted job creation at [Cecil Airport and Spaceport](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/08/31/fscj-cecil-spaceport-jobs-training/) and the growing commerce center that surrounds it, as integral to making Oxford Economics’ forecast for Jacksonville a reality. Howland has also made attracting more aerospace businesses to Cecil to join companies like Boeing and Otto Aerospace a priority of his council presidency. “We will be a top 50 city, mark my words,” Davis said. “It only happens when all get behind what the mayor’s doing. When we all get behind the leadership of growing jobs at Cecil with City Council President Howland. With the vision of the Civic Council in understanding what our DNA is, and creating a momentum with that DNA of what we can be as a community.” [Add Jacksonville Today as a preferred source on Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=jaxtoday.org) [👈☝ What is this?](/2026/04/29/how-to-jacksonville-today-google-results/) --- [Mike Mendenhall](https://jaxtoday.org/author/mike-mendenhall/ "Posts by Mike Mendenhall") Associate Editor [email](mailto:mike@jaxtoday.org) *Jacksonville Today* Associate Editor Mike Mendenhall focuses on Jacksonville City Hall and the Florida Legislature. A native Iowan, he previously led the *Des Moines Business Record* newsroom and served as associate editor of government affairs at the *Jacksonville Daily Record*, where he twice won Florida Press Association TaxWatch Awards for his in-depth coverage of Jacksonville’s city budget. Mike’s work at the *Daily Record* also included reporting on Downtown development, JEA and the city’s independent authorities, and he was a frequent contributor to WJCT News 89.9 and News4Jax. --- ## Keep Reading [![Forested land is shown across the Intercoastal Waterway in St. Johns County. trunks.title: Jacksonville's Culinary Rise: Why It's a Top 5 City for World-Class Ingredients
trunks.script: Jacksonville has seen a significant culinary transformation, becoming a top 5 city for world-class ingredients. This rise is due to the city's commitment to supporting local farmers and producers, enhancing its reputation for high-quality dining experiences.

Gancarski](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/a-g-gancarski/) - [Robin Lumb](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/robin-lumb/) - [Sherry Magill](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/sherry-magill/) - [Cole Pepper](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/cole-pepper/) - [Nikesha Elise Williams](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/nikesha-elise-williams/) [Government & Politics](/category/government-and-politics) ![Mayor Donna Deegan stands at a microphone, speaking about the Oxford Economics ranking.](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-at-Oxford-presser-scaled-e1789503479984-1250x400.webp)![Mayor Donna Deegan stands at a microphone, speaking about the Oxford Economics ranking.](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-at-Oxford-presser-scaled-e1789503479984.webp) Mayor Donna Deegan speaks about Oxford Economics ranking Jacksonville a top 5 city to watch in North America during a news conference Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, at City Hall. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today # ‘World-class ingredients:’ Oxford Economics ranks Jacksonville as a top 5 city to watch By [Mike Mendenhall](/author/mike-mendenhall) Published on September 15, 2026 at 4:48 pm *Free local news and info, in your inbox at 6 a.m. M-F.* [*Sign up for the* Jacksonville Today *newsletter.*](https://jaxtoday.org/signup/) The independent global advisory firm Oxford Economics named Jacksonville a top five North American city to watch in its annual Global Cities Index. Jacksonville’s city and business leaders held a news conference Tuesday at City Hall to celebrate the city’s position on the index and reaffirm their goal to make Jacksonville a top 50 city globally by 2032. Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Mayor Donna Deegan says the city’s improving economic metrics noted in Oxford’s recognition are “not a partisan issue.” The Democratic mayor was joined at the news conference by City Council President Nick Howland, a Republican; Jacksonville Civic Council President and CEO Dennis Whittle; and Daniel Davis, Jax Chamber president and CEO and Deegan’s opponent in the 2023 mayoral election. “Just last week, we opened the UF Jacksonville campus, and we were recognized for having the fastest-growing workforce in the country,” Deegan said. “We already know what’s happening in this city — the investment, the growth, the opportunity we’re building in Downtown and every neighborhood. It’s wonderful to see the rest of the world beginning to recognize it too.” [Article continues below](#most-read-ad-unit) #### More from Jax Today [## Pediatric illnesses illuminate hunger challenge facing Northeast Florida families](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/northeast-florida-childhood-hunger/)[## Second case of West Nile Virus found in Duval County](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/west-nile-virus-duval/)[## St. Johns County reverses course and denies 4,000-home development near Nocatee](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/st-johns-rejects-enclave-development/) Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Oxford Economics’ index currently ranks Jacksonville 97th globally for cities with a population of 4 million or less, a bump from its 119th position on the index last year. The firm weighs the strength of a city’s economics, human capital, quality of life, environment and governance to compile the ranking. The report puts Jacksonville 134th overall out of the 1,000 cities ranked in the study. The Northeast Florida city was in the top five to watch in North America with Boise, Idaho; Durham, North Carolina; San Antonio, Texas; and Edmonton in Alberta, Canada. Oxford Economics findings say 26% of the growth in Jacksonville’s gross domestic product in 2025 can be attributed to the technology sector. It specifically cited the presence of Financial Technology firms like Fidelity National Information Services, Nymbus and Black Knight, as well as large presence from traditional banks like Bank of America, TIAA, Wells Fargo, BBVA and Truist. The city’s total GDP is $148 billion, according to Oxford Economics, or $83,200 per person. That’s based on the regional population of 1.8 million, while Jacksonville proper/Duval County is about 1.1 million people. The Oxford index forecasts a 1% population growth rate per year through 2030, nearly four times the U.S. rate. It highlights the city’s high income per person, smaller rainfall anomalies and large GDP size as strengths. Weaknesses include Jacksonville’s higher crime rate, higher housing expenditures and older age profile. “Jacksonville is a standout city — even by fast-growing Florida standards,” the report states. “Its broad-based growth in recent years has earned it an upgrade in the Global City Index rankings for this year. While much of its growth has been fueled by in-migration and population gains, it is increasingly being recognized on a global scale for its burgeoning finance, tech, fintech, and professional business services sectors.” [Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf)[Download](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf) Howland credited Florida and Jacksonville’s low taxes, relative to Northeastern, Midwestern and Florida peer cities. He also says the city is more “recession proof” with a large share of its jobs in the military, logistics, medical and manufacturing sectors. “We are a low-tax environment. Families and businesses can keep more of the hard-earned money that they make than nearly everywhere else in America,” Howland said. “It’s our quality of life. Our climate, our beach, our rivers — you heard it said — our waterways, our growing culinary scene, our improving Downtown and riverfront, and our improving NFL team. We’re investing in all the right places.” ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-and-Howland-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Mayor Donna Deegan and City Council President Nick Howland attend a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Deegan has been critical of the state Legislature’s push to persuade voters to approve a constitutional amendment to drastically scale back residential property taxes. She said the ranking should be a call for more public-private partnerships and more public and private sector investments in the city’s quality of life to maintain momentum. “It calls for us to attract new people while making sure that the families who built this city can afford to remain here and share in its success,” Deegan said. ### Economic headwinds and Amendment 3 Many of the data points for the ranking were taken from Jacksonville’s 2025 economic numbers. Today, there are some signs that job growth in Northeast Florida could be slowing. The state’s Department of Commerce reported last month that Northeast Florida’s [rate of job growth slowed](https://www.jaxdailyrecord.com/news/2026/aug/24/unemployment-rate-rises-to-49-in-northeast-florida/) in July, and the unemployment rate ticked up from 4.8% in June to 4.9%. The Jacksonville metropolitan area saw 2,900 nonfarm jobs added from July 2025 to July 2026, a 0.4% growth rate. There’s also worry about less property tax revenue for public sector spending by the city if Amendment 3 passes in November. The Jacksonville City Council auditor estimates the Florida property tax cut would mean $300 million less per year for the city by 2027. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Dennis-Whittle-at-Oxford-presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Civic Council CEO Dennis Whittle speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Whittle said when he came to Jacksonville seven years ago, he saw the city’s “world-class ingredients.” The Civic Council CEO says the organization, a panel of 100 of the region’s business executives, will meet to consider a position on the tax referendum soon. He declined to comment directly Tuesday about the tax cut before his board meets. “A lot of people have spoken out against the amendment — the [police and fire unions and a number of sheriffs](https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2026/09/15/florida-sheriffs-firefighters-slam-property-tax-amendment-as-a-train-wreck/). I won’t repeat what they’ve said,” Whittle said. “But I would hate for us to do anything that took the wind out of the sails of what you’re seeing here today,” Whittle said. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Daniel-Davis-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jax Chamber President and CEO Daniel Davis speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Davis touted job creation at [Cecil Airport and Spaceport](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/08/31/fscj-cecil-spaceport-jobs-training/) and the growing commerce center that surrounds it, as integral to making Oxford Economics’ forecast for Jacksonville a reality. Howland has also made attracting more aerospace businesses to Cecil to join companies like Boeing and Otto Aerospace a priority of his council presidency. “We will be a top 50 city, mark my words,” Davis said. “It only happens when all get behind what the mayor’s doing. When we all get behind the leadership of growing jobs at Cecil with City Council President Howland. With the vision of the Civic Council in understanding what our DNA is, and creating a momentum with that DNA of what we can be as a community.” [Add Jacksonville Today as a preferred source on Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=jaxtoday.org) [👈☝ What is this?](/2026/04/29/how-to-jacksonville-today-google-results/) --- [Mike Mendenhall](https://jaxtoday.org/author/mike-mendenhall/ "Posts by Mike Mendenhall") Associate Editor [email](mailto:mike@jaxtoday.org) *Jacksonville Today* Associate Editor Mike Mendenhall focuses on Jacksonville City Hall and the Florida Legislature. Gancarski](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/a-g-gancarski/) - [Robin Lumb](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/robin-lumb/) - [Sherry Magill](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/sherry-magill/) - [Cole Pepper](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/cole-pepper/) - [Nikesha Elise Williams](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/nikesha-elise-williams/) [Government & Politics](/category/government-and-politics) ![Mayor Donna Deegan stands at a microphone, speaking about the Oxford Economics ranking.](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-at-Oxford-presser-scaled-e1789503479984-1250x400.webp)![Mayor Donna Deegan stands at a microphone, speaking about the Oxford Economics ranking.](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-at-Oxford-presser-scaled-e1789503479984.webp) Mayor Donna Deegan speaks about Oxford Economics ranking Jacksonville a top 5 city to watch in North America during a news conference Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, at City Hall. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today # ‘World-class ingredients:’ Oxford Economics ranks Jacksonville as a top 5 city to watch By [Mike Mendenhall](/author/mike-mendenhall) Published on September 15, 2026 at 4:48 pm *Free local news and info, in your inbox at 6 a.m. M-F.* [*Sign up for the* Jacksonville Today *newsletter.*](https://jaxtoday.org/signup/) The independent global advisory firm Oxford Economics named Jacksonville a top five North American city to watch in its annual Global Cities Index. Jacksonville’s city and business leaders held a news conference Tuesday at City Hall to celebrate the city’s position on the index and reaffirm their goal to make Jacksonville a top 50 city globally by 2032. Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Mayor Donna Deegan says the city’s improving economic metrics noted in Oxford’s recognition are “not a partisan issue.” The Democratic mayor was joined at the news conference by City Council President Nick Howland, a Republican; Jacksonville Civic Council President and CEO Dennis Whittle; and Daniel Davis, Jax Chamber president and CEO and Deegan’s opponent in the 2023 mayoral election. “Just last week, we opened the UF Jacksonville campus, and we were recognized for having the fastest-growing workforce in the country,” Deegan said. “We already know what’s happening in this city — the investment, the growth, the opportunity we’re building in Downtown and every neighborhood. It’s wonderful to see the rest of the world beginning to recognize it too.” [Article continues below](#most-read-ad-unit) #### More from Jax Today [## Pediatric illnesses illuminate hunger challenge facing Northeast Florida families](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/northeast-florida-childhood-hunger/)[## Second case of West Nile Virus found in Duval County](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/west-nile-virus-duval/)[## St. Johns County reverses course and denies 4,000-home development near Nocatee](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/st-johns-rejects-enclave-development/) Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Oxford Economics’ index currently ranks Jacksonville 97th globally for cities with a population of 4 million or less, a bump from its 119th position on the index last year. The firm weighs the strength of a city’s economics, human capital, quality of life, environment and governance to compile the ranking. The report puts Jacksonville 134th overall out of the 1,000 cities ranked in the study. The Northeast Florida city was in the top five to watch in North America with Boise, Idaho; Durham, North Carolina; San Antonio, Texas; and Edmonton in Alberta, Canada. Oxford Economics findings say 26% of the growth in Jacksonville’s gross domestic product in 2025 can be attributed to the technology sector. It specifically cited the presence of Financial Technology firms like Fidelity National Information Services, Nymbus and Black Knight, as well as large presence from traditional banks like Bank of America, TIAA, Wells Fargo, BBVA and Truist. The city’s total GDP is $148 billion, according to Oxford Economics, or $83,200 per person. That’s based on the regional population of 1.8 million, while Jacksonville proper/Duval County is about 1.1 million people. The Oxford index forecasts a 1% population growth rate per year through 2030, nearly four times the U.S. rate. It highlights the city’s high income per person, smaller rainfall anomalies and large GDP size as strengths. Weaknesses include Jacksonville’s higher crime rate, higher housing expenditures and older age profile. “Jacksonville is a standout city — even by fast-growing Florida standards,” the report states. “Its broad-based growth in recent years has earned it an upgrade in the Global City Index rankings for this year. While much of its growth has been fueled by in-migration and population gains, it is increasingly being recognized on a global scale for its burgeoning finance, tech, fintech, and professional business services sectors.” [Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf)[Download](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf) Howland credited Florida and Jacksonville’s low taxes, relative to Northeastern, Midwestern and Florida peer cities. He also says the city is more “recession proof” with a large share of its jobs in the military, logistics, medical and manufacturing sectors. “We are a low-tax environment. Families and businesses can keep more of the hard-earned money that they make than nearly everywhere else in America,” Howland said. “It’s our quality of life. Our climate, our beach, our rivers — you heard it said — our waterways, our growing culinary scene, our improving Downtown and riverfront, and our improving NFL team. We’re investing in all the right places.” ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-and-Howland-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Mayor Donna Deegan and City Council President Nick Howland attend a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Deegan has been critical of the state Legislature’s push to persuade voters to approve a constitutional amendment to drastically scale back residential property taxes. She said the ranking should be a call for more public-private partnerships and more public and private sector investments in the city’s quality of life to maintain momentum. “It calls for us to attract new people while making sure that the families who built this city can afford to remain here and share in its success,” Deegan said. ### Economic headwinds and Amendment 3 Many of the data points for the ranking were taken from Jacksonville’s 2025 economic numbers. Today, there are some signs that job growth in Northeast Florida could be slowing. The state’s Department of Commerce reported last month that Northeast Florida’s [rate of job growth slowed](https://www.jaxdailyrecord.com/news/2026/aug/24/unemployment-rate-rises-to-49-in-northeast-florida/) in July, and the unemployment rate ticked up from 4.8% in June to 4.9%. The Jacksonville metropolitan area saw 2,900 nonfarm jobs added from July 2025 to July 2026, a 0.4% growth rate. There’s also worry about less property tax revenue for public sector spending by the city if Amendment 3 passes in November. The Jacksonville City Council auditor estimates the Florida property tax cut would mean $300 million less per year for the city by 2027. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Dennis-Whittle-at-Oxford-presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Civic Council CEO Dennis Whittle speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Whittle said when he came to Jacksonville seven years ago, he saw the city’s “world-class ingredients.” The Civic Council CEO says the organization, a panel of 100 of the region’s business executives, will meet to consider a position on the tax referendum soon. He declined to comment directly Tuesday about the tax cut before his board meets. “A lot of people have spoken out against the amendment — the [police and fire unions and a number of sheriffs](https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2026/09/15/florida-sheriffs-firefighters-slam-property-tax-amendment-as-a-train-wreck/). I won’t repeat what they’ve said,” Whittle said. “But I would hate for us to do anything that took the wind out of the sails of what you’re seeing here today,” Whittle said. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Daniel-Davis-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jax Chamber President and CEO Daniel Davis speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Davis touted job creation at [Cecil Airport and Spaceport](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/08/31/fscj-cecil-spaceport-jobs-training/) and the growing commerce center that surrounds it, as integral to making Oxford Economics’ forecast for Jacksonville a reality. Howland has also made attracting more aerospace businesses to Cecil to join companies like Boeing and Otto Aerospace a priority of his council presidency. “We will be a top 50 city, mark my words,” Davis said. “It only happens when all get behind what the mayor’s doing. When we all get behind the leadership of growing jobs at Cecil with City Council President Howland. With the vision of the Civic Council in understanding what our DNA is, and creating a momentum with that DNA of what we can be as a community.” [Add Jacksonville Today as a preferred source on Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=jaxtoday.org) [👈☝ What is this?](/2026/04/29/how-to-jacksonville-today-google-results/) --- [Mike Mendenhall](https://jaxtoday.org/author/mike-mendenhall/ "Posts by Mike Mendenhall") Associate Editor [email](mailto:mike@jaxtoday.org) *Jacksonville Today* Associate Editor Mike Mendenhall focuses on Jacksonville City Hall and the Florida Legislature. A native Iowan, he previously led the *Des Moines Business Record* newsroom and served as associate editor of government affairs at the *Jacksonville Daily Record*, where he twice won Florida Press Association TaxWatch Awards for his in-depth coverage of Jacksonville’s city budget. Mike’s work at the *Daily Record* also included reporting on Downtown development, JEA and the city’s independent authorities, and he was a frequent contributor to WJCT News 89.9 and News4Jax. --- ## Keep Reading [![Forested land is shown across the Intercoastal Waterway in St. Johns County. trunks.title: Jacksonville's Culinary Rise: Why It's a Top 5 City for World-Class Ingredients
trunks.script: Jacksonville has seen a significant culinary transformation, emerging as a top 5 city for world-class ingredients. Local chefs and farmers are collaborating to offer unique dining experiences. The city's food scene is highlighted in various sections of JaxToday, including The Food Section and What to Do, showcasing the diverse and high-quality culinary offerings.

Gancarski](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/a-g-gancarski/) - [Robin Lumb](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/robin-lumb/) - [Sherry Magill](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/sherry-magill/) - [Cole Pepper](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/cole-pepper/) - [Nikesha Elise Williams](https://jaxtoday.org/category/perspectives/nikesha-elise-williams/) [Government & Politics](/category/government-and-politics) ![Mayor Donna Deegan stands at a microphone, speaking about the Oxford Economics ranking.](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-at-Oxford-presser-scaled-e1789503479984-1250x400.webp)![Mayor Donna Deegan stands at a microphone, speaking about the Oxford Economics ranking.](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-at-Oxford-presser-scaled-e1789503479984.webp) Mayor Donna Deegan speaks about Oxford Economics ranking Jacksonville a top 5 city to watch in North America during a news conference Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, at City Hall. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today # ‘World-class ingredients:’ Oxford Economics ranks Jacksonville as a top 5 city to watch By [Mike Mendenhall](/author/mike-mendenhall) Published on September 15, 2026 at 4:48 pm *Free local news and info, in your inbox at 6 a.m. M-F.* [*Sign up for the* Jacksonville Today *newsletter.*](https://jaxtoday.org/signup/) The independent global advisory firm Oxford Economics named Jacksonville a top five North American city to watch in its annual Global Cities Index. Jacksonville’s city and business leaders held a news conference Tuesday at City Hall to celebrate the city’s position on the index and reaffirm their goal to make Jacksonville a top 50 city globally by 2032. Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Mayor Donna Deegan says the city’s improving economic metrics noted in Oxford’s recognition are “not a partisan issue.” The Democratic mayor was joined at the news conference by City Council President Nick Howland, a Republican; Jacksonville Civic Council President and CEO Dennis Whittle; and Daniel Davis, Jax Chamber president and CEO and Deegan’s opponent in the 2023 mayoral election. “Just last week, we opened the UF Jacksonville campus, and we were recognized for having the fastest-growing workforce in the country,” Deegan said. “We already know what’s happening in this city — the investment, the growth, the opportunity we’re building in Downtown and every neighborhood. It’s wonderful to see the rest of the world beginning to recognize it too.” [Article continues below](#most-read-ad-unit) #### More from Jax Today [## Pediatric illnesses illuminate hunger challenge facing Northeast Florida families](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/northeast-florida-childhood-hunger/)[## Second case of West Nile Virus found in Duval County](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/west-nile-virus-duval/)[## St. Johns County reverses course and denies 4,000-home development near Nocatee](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/st-johns-rejects-enclave-development/) Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Oxford Economics’ index currently ranks Jacksonville 97th globally for cities with a population of 4 million or less, a bump from its 119th position on the index last year. The firm weighs the strength of a city’s economics, human capital, quality of life, environment and governance to compile the ranking. The report puts Jacksonville 134th overall out of the 1,000 cities ranked in the study. The Northeast Florida city was in the top five to watch in North America with Boise, Idaho; Durham, North Carolina; San Antonio, Texas; and Edmonton in Alberta, Canada. Oxford Economics findings say 26% of the growth in Jacksonville’s gross domestic product in 2025 can be attributed to the technology sector. It specifically cited the presence of Financial Technology firms like Fidelity National Information Services, Nymbus and Black Knight, as well as large presence from traditional banks like Bank of America, TIAA, Wells Fargo, BBVA and Truist. The city’s total GDP is $148 billion, according to Oxford Economics, or $83,200 per person. That’s based on the regional population of 1.8 million, while Jacksonville proper/Duval County is about 1.1 million people. The Oxford index forecasts a 1% population growth rate per year through 2030, nearly four times the U.S. rate. It highlights the city’s high income per person, smaller rainfall anomalies and large GDP size as strengths. Weaknesses include Jacksonville’s higher crime rate, higher housing expenditures and older age profile. “Jacksonville is a standout city — even by fast-growing Florida standards,” the report states. “Its broad-based growth in recent years has earned it an upgrade in the Global City Index rankings for this year. While much of its growth has been fueled by in-migration and population gains, it is increasingly being recognized on a global scale for its burgeoning finance, tech, fintech, and professional business services sectors.” [Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf)[Download](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf) Howland credited Florida and Jacksonville’s low taxes, relative to Northeastern, Midwestern and Florida peer cities. He also says the city is more “recession proof” with a large share of its jobs in the military, logistics, medical and manufacturing sectors. “We are a low-tax environment. Families and businesses can keep more of the hard-earned money that they make than nearly everywhere else in America,” Howland said. “It’s our quality of life. Our climate, our beach, our rivers — you heard it said — our waterways, our growing culinary scene, our improving Downtown and riverfront, and our improving NFL team. We’re investing in all the right places.” ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-and-Howland-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Mayor Donna Deegan and City Council President Nick Howland attend a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Deegan has been critical of the state Legislature’s push to persuade voters to approve a constitutional amendment to drastically scale back residential property taxes. She said the ranking should be a call for more public-private partnerships and more public and private sector investments in the city’s quality of life to maintain momentum. “It calls for us to attract new people while making sure that the families who built this city can afford to remain here and share in its success,” Deegan said. ### Economic headwinds and Amendment 3 Many of the data points for the ranking were taken from Jacksonville’s 2025 economic numbers. Today, there are some signs that job growth in Northeast Florida could be slowing. The state’s Department of Commerce reported last month that Northeast Florida’s [rate of job growth slowed](https://www.jaxdailyrecord.com/news/2026/aug/24/unemployment-rate-rises-to-49-in-northeast-florida/) in July, and the unemployment rate ticked up from 4.8% in June to 4.9%. The Jacksonville metropolitan area saw 2,900 nonfarm jobs added from July 2025 to July 2026, a 0.4% growth rate. There’s also worry about less property tax revenue for public sector spending by the city if Amendment 3 passes in November. The Jacksonville City Council auditor estimates the Florida property tax cut would mean $300 million less per year for the city by 2027. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Dennis-Whittle-at-Oxford-presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Civic Council CEO Dennis Whittle speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Whittle said when he came to Jacksonville seven years ago, he saw the city’s “world-class ingredients.” The Civic Council CEO says the organization, a panel of 100 of the region’s business executives, will meet to consider a position on the tax referendum soon. He declined to comment directly Tuesday about the tax cut before his board meets. “A lot of people have spoken out against the amendment — the [police and fire unions and a number of sheriffs](https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2026/09/15/florida-sheriffs-firefighters-slam-property-tax-amendment-as-a-train-wreck/). I won’t repeat what they’ve said,” Whittle said. “But I would hate for us to do anything that took the wind out of the sails of what you’re seeing here today,” Whittle said. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Daniel-Davis-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jax Chamber President and CEO Daniel Davis speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Davis touted job creation at [Cecil Airport and Spaceport](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/08/31/fscj-cecil-spaceport-jobs-training/) and the growing commerce center that surrounds it, as integral to making Oxford Economics’ forecast for Jacksonville a reality. Howland has also made attracting more aerospace businesses to Cecil to join companies like Boeing and Otto Aerospace a priority of his council presidency. “We will be a top 50 city, mark my words,” Davis said. “It only happens when all get behind what the mayor’s doing. When we all get behind the leadership of growing jobs at Cecil with City Council President Howland. With the vision of the Civic Council in understanding what our DNA is, and creating a momentum with that DNA of what we can be as a community.” [Add Jacksonville Today as a preferred source on Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=jaxtoday.org) [👈☝ What is this?](/2026/04/29/how-to-jacksonville-today-google-results/) --- [Mike Mendenhall](https://jaxtoday.org/author/mike-mendenhall/ "Posts by Mike Mendenhall") Associate Editor [email](mailto:mike@jaxtoday.org) *Jacksonville Today* Associate Editor Mike Mendenhall focuses on Jacksonville City Hall and the Florida Legislature. A native Iowan, he previously led the *Des Moines Business Record* newsroom and served as associate editor of government affairs at the *Jacksonville Daily Record*, where he twice won Florida Press Association TaxWatch Awards for his in-depth coverage of Jacksonville’s city budget. Mike’s work at the *Daily Record* also included reporting on Downtown development, JEA and the city’s independent authorities, and he was a frequent contributor to WJCT News 89.9 and News4Jax. --- ## Keep Reading [![Forested land is shown across the Intercoastal Waterway in St. Johns County. trunks.title: Jacksonville's Culinary Rise: Why It's a Top 5 City for World-Class Ingredients
trunks.script: Jacksonville has emerged as a top city for world-class ingredients, thanks to its strategic location and commitment to culinary excellence. The city's proximity to the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean provides access to fresh seafood, while its inland waterways offer a variety of freshwater fish. Local farmers and producers contribute to the city's vibrant food scene, ensuring that restaurants can source high-quality, locally grown produce. This combination of fresh, locally sourced ingredients has made Jacksonville a must-visit destination for food enthusiasts.

Jacksonville’s city and business leaders held a news conference Tuesday at City Hall to celebrate the city’s position on the index and reaffirm their goal to make Jacksonville a top 50 city globally by 2032. Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Mayor Donna Deegan says the city’s improving economic metrics noted in Oxford’s recognition are “not a partisan issue.” The Democratic mayor was joined at the news conference by City Council President Nick Howland, a Republican; Jacksonville Civic Council President and CEO Dennis Whittle; and Daniel Davis, Jax Chamber president and CEO and Deegan’s opponent in the 2023 mayoral election. “Just last week, we opened the UF Jacksonville campus, and we were recognized for having the fastest-growing workforce in the country,” Deegan said. “We already know what’s happening in this city — the investment, the growth, the opportunity we’re building in Downtown and every neighborhood. It’s wonderful to see the rest of the world beginning to recognize it too.” [Article continues below](#most-read-ad-unit) #### More from Jax Today [## Pediatric illnesses illuminate hunger challenge facing Northeast Florida families](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/northeast-florida-childhood-hunger/)[## Second case of West Nile Virus found in Duval County](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/west-nile-virus-duval/)[## St. Johns County reverses course and denies 4,000-home development near Nocatee](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/09/15/st-johns-rejects-enclave-development/) Jacksonville Today thanks our sponsors. [Become one.](/corporate-marketing/) Oxford Economics’ index currently ranks Jacksonville 97th globally for cities with a population of 4 million or less, a bump from its 119th position on the index last year. The firm weighs the strength of a city’s economics, human capital, quality of life, environment and governance to compile the ranking. The report puts Jacksonville 134th overall out of the 1,000 cities ranked in the study. The Northeast Florida city was in the top five to watch in North America with Boise, Idaho; Durham, North Carolina; San Antonio, Texas; and Edmonton in Alberta, Canada. Oxford Economics findings say 26% of the growth in Jacksonville’s gross domestic product in 2025 can be attributed to the technology sector. It specifically cited the presence of Financial Technology firms like Fidelity National Information Services, Nymbus and Black Knight, as well as large presence from traditional banks like Bank of America, TIAA, Wells Fargo, BBVA and Truist. The city’s total GDP is $148 billion, according to Oxford Economics, or $83,200 per person. That’s based on the regional population of 1.8 million, while Jacksonville proper/Duval County is about 1.1 million people. The Oxford index forecasts a 1% population growth rate per year through 2030, nearly four times the U.S. rate. It highlights the city’s high income per person, smaller rainfall anomalies and large GDP size as strengths. Weaknesses include Jacksonville’s higher crime rate, higher housing expenditures and older age profile. “Jacksonville is a standout city — even by fast-growing Florida standards,” the report states. “Its broad-based growth in recent years has earned it an upgrade in the Global City Index rankings for this year. While much of its growth has been fueled by in-migration and population gains, it is increasingly being recognized on a global scale for its burgeoning finance, tech, fintech, and professional business services sectors.” [Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf)[Download](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Oxford-Economics-Global-Cities-Index-2026-report.pdf) Howland credited Florida and Jacksonville’s low taxes, relative to Northeastern, Midwestern and Florida peer cities. He also says the city is more “recession proof” with a large share of its jobs in the military, logistics, medical and manufacturing sectors. “We are a low-tax environment. Families and businesses can keep more of the hard-earned money that they make than nearly everywhere else in America,” Howland said. “It’s our quality of life. Our climate, our beach, our rivers — you heard it said — our waterways, our growing culinary scene, our improving Downtown and riverfront, and our improving NFL team. We’re investing in all the right places.” ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Deegan-and-Howland-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Mayor Donna Deegan and City Council President Nick Howland attend a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Deegan has been critical of the state Legislature’s push to persuade voters to approve a constitutional amendment to drastically scale back residential property taxes. She said the ranking should be a call for more public-private partnerships and more public and private sector investments in the city’s quality of life to maintain momentum. “It calls for us to attract new people while making sure that the families who built this city can afford to remain here and share in its success,” Deegan said. ### Economic headwinds and Amendment 3 Many of the data points for the ranking were taken from Jacksonville’s 2025 economic numbers. Today, there are some signs that job growth in Northeast Florida could be slowing. The state’s Department of Commerce reported last month that Northeast Florida’s [rate of job growth slowed](https://www.jaxdailyrecord.com/news/2026/aug/24/unemployment-rate-rises-to-49-in-northeast-florida/) in July, and the unemployment rate ticked up from 4.8% in June to 4.9%. The Jacksonville metropolitan area saw 2,900 nonfarm jobs added from July 2025 to July 2026, a 0.4% growth rate. There’s also worry about less property tax revenue for public sector spending by the city if Amendment 3 passes in November. The Jacksonville City Council auditor estimates the Florida property tax cut would mean $300 million less per year for the city by 2027. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Dennis-Whittle-at-Oxford-presser-1024x768.webp) Jacksonville Civic Council CEO Dennis Whittle speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Whittle said when he came to Jacksonville seven years ago, he saw the city’s “world-class ingredients.” The Civic Council CEO says the organization, a panel of 100 of the region’s business executives, will meet to consider a position on the tax referendum soon. He declined to comment directly Tuesday about the tax cut before his board meets. “A lot of people have spoken out against the amendment — the [police and fire unions and a number of sheriffs](https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2026/09/15/florida-sheriffs-firefighters-slam-property-tax-amendment-as-a-train-wreck/). I won’t repeat what they’ve said,” Whittle said. “But I would hate for us to do anything that took the wind out of the sails of what you’re seeing here today,” Whittle said. ![](https://jaxtoday.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Daniel-Davis-at-Oxford-Presser-1024x768.webp) Jax Chamber President and CEO Daniel Davis speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, about Oxford Economics naming Jacksonville at top five city to watch in North America. | Mike Mendenhall, Jacksonville Today Davis touted job creation at [Cecil Airport and Spaceport](https://jaxtoday.org/2026/08/31/fscj-cecil-spaceport-jobs-training/) and the growing commerce center that surrounds it, as integral to making Oxford Economics’ forecast for Jacksonville a reality. Howland has also made attracting more aerospace businesses to Cecil to join companies like Boeing and Otto Aerospace a priority of his council presidency. “We will be a top 50 city, mark my words,” Davis said. “It only happens when all get behind what the mayor’s doing. When we all get behind the leadership of growing jobs at Cecil with City Council President Howland. trunks.title: Jacksonville's Culinary Rise: Why It's a Top 5 City for World-Class Ingredients
trunks.script: Jacksonville has seen a significant culinary transformation, emerging as a top city for world-class ingredients. Local chefs and restaurateurs are leveraging the region's rich agricultural resources and diverse seafood to create innovative dishes. The city's commitment to supporting local farmers and fishermen ensures a steady supply of fresh, high-quality produce and seafood. This focus on local sourcing has not only enhanced the dining experience but also boosted the local economy.
